editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: Now the book before this, which is the tenth of the whole composition, ended its narrative of events with the year preceding the crossing of Xerxes into Europe, and with the public speeches delivered in the general assembly of the Greeks at Corinth concerning the alliance of Gelon with the Greeks. In this book, completing the continuous course of the history, we shall begin with the expedition of Xerxes against the Greeks, and we shall conclude with the year preceding the expedition of the Athenians against Cyprus under the command of Cimon.

One might justly be perplexed, fixing one's mind on the inconsistency in human life; for neither of the things reckoned good is found to be given to men whole and entire, nor of the evils any that is complete without some admixture of usefulness. The proofs of this it will be possible to take by fixing the mind on the deeds done in former times, and especially on the greatest.

If we were composing a history like the others, it would be possible, after discussing certain matters in the preface as far as was opportune, thus to bring the account over to the continuous deeds; for, taking up only a little time for the writing, we should have the opportunity to add the fruit that comes from the prefaces.

It is likely that all men hear with displeasure the slanders spoken against them; for even those whose own wickedness is so manifest in every respect that they cannot deny it nevertheless grow indignant when they meet with censure and try to bring forward arguments against the accusation. Therefore one must by every means guard against doing anything base, all men, but most of all those who reach out for positions of leadership or who have come to share in some conspicuous fortune; 1.2. for the life of such men, being open to view because of its eminence, is in everything unable to conceal its own want of judgement; so let no one of those who have attained any pre-eminence hope, if he commits great wrongs, to pass to the end unrebuked. For even if in his own lifetime he should escape the reckoning that comes from rebuke, let him expect that afterward the truth will come upon him, proclaiming with frankness the things long passed over in silence. 1.3. It is a hard thing, then, for base men to leave behind to later generations, after their own death, as it were an undying image of their whole life; for even if, as some of the philosophers babble, the things after death are nothing to us, nevertheless the life that has gone before becomes far the worse for being remembered through all eternity for evil. Of these things clear examples may be taken by those who read the several events contained in this book. 2.1. For among the Athenians thirty tyrants arose who through their own greed both involved their fatherland in great disasters and themselves, quickly losing their power, left behind an undying reproach against themselves; while the Lacedaemonians, having acquired the undisputed leadership of Greece, were then deprived of it when they undertook to perform unjust deeds against their allies. For the supremacy of leaders is preserved by goodwill and justice, but is dissolved by acts of injustice and by the hatred of their subjects. 2.2. In like manner also Dionysius the tyrant of the Syracusans, although he became the most fortunate of rulers, yet while he lived never ceased to be plotted against, and through fear was compelled to wear an iron breastplate beneath his tunic; and when he died he left his own life behind as the greatest example for slander through all eternity. 2.3. But concerning these matters we shall record each in its proper time more clearly; now we shall turn to what follows upon what has already been narrated, defining only the chronology. 2.4. In the books before this one we recorded the events from the capture of Troy down to the dissolution both of the Peloponnesian War and of the Athenian supremacy, traversing seven hundred and seventy-nine years; in this book, continuing the connected narrative, we shall begin with the establishment of the Thirty Tyrants at Athens, and shall end with the capture of Rome by the Gauls, embracing eighteen years. 3.1. There being anarchy at Athens because of the dissolution of its supremacy, it was the seven hundred and eightieth year after the capture of Troy, and at Rome four military tribunes succeeded to the consular office, Gaius Fulvius, Gaius Servilius, Gaius Valerius, and Numerius Fabius; and in this year the ninety-fourth Olympiad was celebrated, in which Corcinas the Larissaean was victor. 3.2. About these times the Athenians, worn down by war, made a treaty with the Lacedaemonians, by the terms of which they were to tear down the walls of the city and to use their ancestral constitution. And the walls they did pull down, but over the constitution they fell into dispute with one another. 3.3. For those who reached out for oligarchy said that the ancient order ought to be renewed, under which a very few presided over the whole; while the majority, being lovers of democracy, brought forward the constitution of their fathers, and declared this to be by common agreement a democracy. 3.4. A dispute about these matters arising for some days, those who favoured oligarchy sent envoys to Lysander the Spartan—for he, when the war was concluded, had been dispatched to order the affairs of the cities, and oligarchies were being established in most of them—hoping, as was reasonable, that he would join in supporting their undertaking. They sailed therefore to Samos; for there Lysander happened to be staying, having lately taken the city. 3.5. When they urged him to cooperate, he gave his consent, and appointed Thorax the Spartan as harmost of Samos, while he himself with a hundred ships sailed to the Piraeus. There, calling an assembly, he advised the Athenians to choose thirty men who should preside over the constitution and administer all the affairs of the city. 3.6. When Theramenes spoke against this and read aloud the treaty, in which it had been agreed that they should use their ancestral constitution, and said that it was a terrible thing if contrary to their oaths they were to be deprived of their freedom, Lysander declared that the treaty had been broken by the Athenians; for they had torn down the walls later than the days agreed upon. He also held over Theramenes the gravest threats, saying he would kill him if he did not cease opposing the Lacedaemonians. 3.7. Therefore Theramenes and the people, struck with dismay, were compelled by show of hands to abolish the democracy. So thirty men were chosen who should administer the common affairs of the city, in name magistrates, but in their actions tyrants. 4.1. The people, seeing the fairness of Theramenes and thinking that by his good character the greed of those in power would to some extent be held in check, elected him too among the thirty rulers. The men chosen were required both to establish a council and the other magistracies, and to draw up the laws by which they intended to govern. 4.2. Now the matters concerning the legislation they kept putting off, always providing plausible excuses, but the council and the other offices they filled from their own friends, so that these were called magistrates but were in fact the servants of the Thirty. And at first, handing over to trial the most wicked men in the city, they condemned them to death; and up to this point what was being done was pleasing to the most fair-minded of the citizens. 4.3. After this, wishing to act more violently and lawlessly, they asked the Lacedaemonians for a garrison, saying that they would establish a constitution advantageous to them. For they knew that they could not carry out murders without foreign arms; for all would cling to the common safety. 4.4. When the Lacedaemonians had sent a garrison and Callibius to command it, the Thirty courted the garrison commander with gifts and other kindnesses, and selecting from among the wealthy those who suited their purpose they arrested them as revolutionaries, and putting them to death confiscated their properties. 4.5. When Theramenes opposed his colleagues and, together with those who clung to the common safety, threatened to defend himself, the Thirty assembled the council. Critias, presiding over them and accusing Theramenes at length of betraying this constitution of which he himself was a willing partner, Theramenes took up the discourse and, defending himself on each point, won over the whole council to goodwill. 4.6. But Critias and his party, fearing the man lest he should ever overthrow the oligarchy, set around soldiers with drawn swords and seized Theramenes. 4.7. He, anticipating them, leaped up to the Hestia of the council, and said that he was taking refuge with the gods, not because he thought to be saved, but eager to fasten upon those who would slay him the guilt of impiety toward the gods. 5.1. When the servants came forward and dragged him away, Theramenes bore his misfortune nobly, inasmuch as he had shared in philosophy to a considerable degree with Socrates, while the rest of the multitude pitied Theramenes in his ill fortune, yet did not dare to help him, since many men stood about with arms. 5.2. But Socrates the philosopher and two of his intimates ran up and attempted to hinder the servants. Theramenes, however, asked them to do none of these things; for he said that he praised their friendship and their courage, but that it would be the greatest calamity for himself if he should be the cause of death to men so kindly disposed toward him. 5.3. So Socrates and his companions, having no other helper and seeing the violence of the men in power increasing, kept quiet. And those to whom it had been ordered dragged Theramenes from the altars and hauled him through the middle of the market-place to his death; 5.4. and the multitude, terrified by the arms of the garrison, grieved with the unfortunate man, and wept both at his misfortune and at their own slavery; for each of the lowly, seeing the virtue of Theramenes so insulted, concluded that their own weakness would be expended without any account. 5.5. After his death the Thirty, selecting the wealthy, cast false charges upon them, and murdering them plundered their properties. They put to death also Niceratus, the son of Nicias who had been general against the Syracusans, a man fair and humane toward all, and in wealth and reputation almost first of all the Athenians; 5.6. wherefore it came to pass that every household grieved together at the man's death, the memory of his fairness leading them to tears. But the tyrants did not cease from their lawlessness; nay, much rather, as their madness took on increase, they slaughtered sixty of the wealthiest of the foreigners, that they might gain control of their money, while of the citizens, who were being put to death day by day, those well provided in their means almost all fled from the city. 5.7. They put to death also Autolycus, a man of free speech, and in general they picked out the most refined. To such a degree did they ruin the city that more than half of the Athenians fled. 6.1. The Lacedaemonians, seeing the city of the Athenians brought low, and never wishing the Athenians to grow strong, rejoiced and made their disposition manifest; for they voted that the Athenian exiles should be liable to seizure for the Thirty out of all Greece, and that whoever should hinder this should be liable to a fine of five talents. 6.2. The decree being a terrible one, the other cities, struck with dread at the weight of the Spartans, obeyed; but the Argives first, hating the cruelty of the Lacedaemonians and pitying the fortunes of the luckless, received the exiles humanely. 6.3. The Thebans also voted that there should be a penalty for him who saw an exile being led away and did not help to the best of his ability. Such, then, was the state of affairs concerning the Athenians.

Throughout the whole work being accustomed to use the frankness usual to history, and to add the just praise to good men upon their noble deeds, and to deem the base, when they do wrong, worthy of just censure, we think that by such a method we shall both incite those well disposed by nature toward virtue, through the immortality conferred by glory, to undertake the noblest deeds, and shall turn away those of the contrary disposition, by the fitting reproaches, from their impulse toward wickedness. 1.2. Therefore, being come in our writing to those times in which the Lacedaemonians, unexpectedly defeated at Leuctra, fell into a great calamity, and again, stumbling at Mantinea, lost beyond hope the leadership of the Greeks, we think it our duty to preserve the principle of our writing and to make the fitting censure of the Lacedaemonians. 1.3. For who would not consider them worthy of accusation, who, having received from their forefathers a leadership most nobly founded, and preserved through the virtue of their ancestors for more than five hundred years, then looked on while it was dissolved through their own folly—not unreasonably? For those who had lived before them had acquired by many toils and great dangers so great a glory, dealing fairly and humanely with their subjects; but the later generations, dealing violently and harshly with their allies, and besides constituting unjust and arrogant wars against the Greeks, not unreasonably lost their rule through their own follies. 1.4. For in their misfortunes the hatred of the wronged found an opportunity to take vengeance on those who had wronged them first, and upon men who from their forefathers had been unconquered there followed so great a contempt as is likely to arise against those who destroy the virtues of their forefathers. 1.5. Therefore the Thebans, who before for many generations had been subject to their betters, then unexpectedly conquering these became leaders of the Greeks, while the Lacedaemonians, after the loss of their leadership, were never able to recover the dignity of their ancestors. 1.6. Having censured them sufficiently, we shall pass to the continuous narrative of our history, after first defining the times proper to the writing. The book before this, being the fourteenth of the whole work, ended its events at the enslavement of the Rhegians by Dionysius and the capture of Rome by the Gauls, which occurred in the year before the expedition of the Persians into Cyprus against King Evagoras; in this book, beginning from this war, we shall end at the year before the kingship of Philip the son of Amyntas. 2.1. For in the archonship at Athens of Mystichides the Romans appointed three military tribunes in place of the consuls, Marcus Furius, and besides Gaius and Aemilius. In this year Artaxerxes the King of the Persians campaigned against Evagoras the king of Cyprus. Having for a long time been occupied with the preparations for the war, he assembled a great force both naval and infantry; for the infantry army was thirty myriads with the cavalry, and he constructed more than three hundred triremes. 2.2. He appointed as generals of the infantry force Orontes his son-in-law, and of the naval force Tiribazus, a man enjoying great esteem among the Persians. These, taking over the forces at Phocaea and Cyme, came to Cilicia, and crossing over to Cyprus carried on the war vigorously. 2.3. Evagoras made an alliance with Acoris the king of the Egyptians, who was an enemy of the Persians, and obtained from him a considerable force; and from Hecatomnus the ruler of Caria, who secretly cooperated with him, he received a quantity of money for the maintenance of foreign forces; likewise too the others who were ill disposed toward the Persians, some secretly, some openly, he drew into sharing in the Persian war. 2.4. He was master in Cyprus of almost all the cities, and in Phoenicia of Tyre and certain others. He had ninety triremes, of which twenty were Tyrian and seventy Cyprian, and of his own soldiers six thousand, and from the allies far more than these. Besides these he enlisted many mercenaries, having abundance of money. The king of the Arabs also sent him not a few soldiers, and certain others who were under suspicion with the King of the Persians. 3.1. He, then, having so great resources, went down confidently to the war. And first, having not a few piratical ships, he lay in wait for the provisions of the enemy as they were conveyed, and some of them he destroyed at sea, others he prevented, and some he carried off. Therefore, the merchants not daring to convey grain to Cyprus, and great forces being gathered on the island, a famine quickly held the camp of the Persians. 3.2. The scarcity leading to faction, the mercenaries of the Persians, rushing upon the commanders and slaying some, filled the camp with tumult and faction. Hardly did the generals of the Persians and the leader of the naval force, named Glos, put an end to the faction. 3.3. Sailing out with the whole fleet and conveying a quantity of grain from Cilicia, they provided much abundance of food. To Evagoras a sufficient quantity of grain King Acoris conveyed from Egypt, and money and the rest of a sufficient supply he sent out. 3.4. Evagoras, seeing himself far inferior in naval force, manned sixty other ships and sent for fifty from Acoris out of Egypt, so as to have in all two hundred triremes. Adorning these strikingly for a sea-battle, and making continual trials and exercises, he prepared for a sea-fight. Therefore, when the royal fleet was sailing along to Citium, attacking the ships unexpectedly, he had many advantages over the Persians. 3.5. For he attacked with ships drawn up in order against ships in disorder, and fighting with men forewarned against men unprepared, he immediately at the first encounter prepared the victory beforehand; for, attacking with his triremes in close order against ships scattered and in confusion, some he destroyed, others he mastered. 3.6. Nevertheless, the admiral of the Persians, Glos, and the other commanders withstanding nobly, a fierce sea-battle took place, in which Evagoras at first had the advantage, but afterward, Glos bearing on with weight and fighting nobly, it came to pass that the men of Evagoras fled and lost many of their triremes. 4.1. The Persians, victorious in the sea-battle, gathered both forces at the city Citium. Setting out from this, they constituted a siege against Salamis, and ravaged the city both by land and by sea. 4.2. Tiribazus, after the sea-battle, crossing to Cilicia and going from there to the King, both reported the victory and brought back two thousand talents for the war; while Evagoras, before the sea-battle, having engaged on land by the sea with a part of the infantry force, had had the advantage and become confident for the future, but, having stumbled in the sea-battle and being shut up in a siege, was despondent. 4.3. Nevertheless, deciding to hold to the war, he left his son Pnytagoras, making him leader of all affairs in Cyprus, while he himself, taking ten triremes, by night unobserved by the enemy sailed out of Salamis. Conveyed to Egypt and meeting the king, he urged him to hold firmly to the war and to consider the war against the Persians a common one.

In all historical works it is fitting that the writers should embrace in their books the self-contained actions of cities or of kings, complete from beginning to end; for in this way above all do we judge history to become easy to remember and clear to those who read it.

In all historical works it is fitting that the writers should embrace in their books actions complete in themselves; for in this way above all does history become, in my judgement, easy to remember and clear to those who read it.

When Calliades was archon at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Spurius Cassius and Proclus Verginius Tricostus; and among the Eleans the seventy-fifth Olympiad was celebrated, in which Astylus of Syracuse won the stadium-race. In their time Xerxes the king made his expedition against Greece for the following reason.

For the expedition of Xerxes the king of the Persians against Greece, by reason of the magnitude of its forces, brought the greatest fear upon the Greeks, since they were about to fight for their enslavement; and, the Greek cities in Asia having been already enslaved beforehand, all supposed that the cities in Greece too would experience the like fortune.

But since in a few books we have undertaken not only to write the deeds as far as we are able, but also to comprehend a period of more than eleven hundred years, it is necessary, having passed over the lengthy discourse of the prefaces, to come to the deeds themselves, saying only this beforehand, that in the preceding six books we have recorded the deeds from the Trojan times down to the war voted by the Athenians against the Syracusans, to which, from the capture of Troy, are seven hundred and sixty-eight years;

For unfinished actions, having no continuous link between their beginnings and their conclusion, cut short the eagerness of those who love reading, whereas those that embrace the continuity of the narrative down to its end present an account of events that is fully rounded out. And when the very nature of the events lends its aid to the writers, then indeed one ought not at all to depart from this purpose.

The book before this one, being the sixteenth of the whole work, took its beginning from the reign of Philip the son of Amyntas. It included all the deeds of Philip down to his death, and those of the other kings, nations, and cities that took place during the years of his reign, which numbered twenty-four.

Mardonius the Persian was a cousin and brother-in-law of Xerxes, and was most admired among the Persians for his intelligence and courage. This man, being elated in spirit and at the height of his prime, longed to lead great armies; and so he persuaded Xerxes to enslave the Greeks, who were always hostile to the Persians.

But the war having taken, contrary to expectation, a paradoxical end, not only were the inhabitants of Greece freed from the dangers, but they also acquired great glory, and so great a prosperity filled every Greek city that all marveled at the change to the opposite.

and in this book, filling in the continuous time, we shall begin from the expedition against the Syracusans and conclude at the beginning of the second war of the Carthaginians against Dionysius the tyrant of the Syracusans.

For this reason we too, now that we have come to the deeds of Philip the son of Amyntas, shall undertake to embrace within this book the actions accomplished by this king. For he reigned over the Macedonians for twenty-four years, and starting from the slenderest resources he built his own kingdom into the greatest of the dominions in Europe, and taking over Macedonia when it was enslaved to the Illyrians, he made it mistress of many great nations and cities.

In this book, as we record the events that follow upon those, we shall begin with the reign of Alexander; and, embracing the deeds of this king down to his death, we shall set down together with them whatever was accomplished in the same period in the known parts of the inhabited world. For in this way above all do we suppose that the events will be easy to remember, set out under their main heads and having their conclusion continuous with their beginnings.

And Xerxes, persuaded by him and wishing to drive all the Greeks from their homes, sent an embassy to the Carthaginians about joint action and made an agreement with them, to the effect that he himself should make war on the Greeks who dwell in Greece, while the Carthaginians should at the same time prepare great forces and subdue those of the Greeks who dwelt about Sicily and Italy.

For from these times, for fifty years, Greece received much increase toward prosperity. For in these times the arts grew because of the prosperity, and then the greatest craftsmen are recorded to have arisen, among whom is Pheidias the sculptor; likewise too the things pertaining to education advanced greatly, and philosophy and rhetoric were held in honor among all the Greeks, but especially among the Athenians.

And through his own valour he took over the leadership of all Greece, the cities submitting to him of their own will; and after defeating those who had plundered the temple at Delphi and giving aid to the oracle, he gained a seat in the council of the Amphictyons, and because of his piety toward the gods he received as his prize the votes of the conquered Phocians.

In a short span of time this king accomplished great deeds, and through his own intelligence and courage he surpassed in the magnitude of his achievements all the kings whose memory has been handed down from the beginning of time.

In accordance with the agreements, then, the Carthaginians, having gathered a great quantity of money, collected mercenaries from Italy and Liguria, and further from Galatia and Iberia; and in addition to these they enrolled citizen forces from all Libya and from Carthage. Finally, after spending three years on their preparations, they assembled more than three hundred thousand foot-soldiers and two hundred ships.

For there were philosophers, those about Socrates and Plato and Aristotle; orators, Pericles and Isocrates and his pupils; and likewise men renowned for generalship, Miltiades, Themistocles, Aristides, Cimon, Myronides, and many others, about whom it would be long to write.

And after subduing the Illyrians and the Paeonians and the Thracians and the Scythians and all the nations bordering upon these, he set himself to overthrow the kingdom of the Persians; and having transported forces into Asia he was freeing the Greek cities, when, cut short by fate, he left behind forces so great and of such quality that his son Alexander had no need of allies for the overthrow of the Persian empire.

For in the space of twelve years he subdued no small part of Europe and almost the whole of Asia, and so won, with good reason, a fame far-resounding and equal to that of the heroes and demigods of old. But there is no need for us in our preface to anticipate any of this king's achievements; for the particular deeds themselves will sufficiently reveal the greatness of his renown. Alexander, then, being descended on his father's side from Heracles and on his mother's from the Aeacidae, possessed by birth a nature and a virtue worthy of the high renown of his ancestors. We, however, having set out the dates appropriate to our narrative, shall turn to the events that belong to the history before us.

And these things he accomplished not through fortune but through his own valour. For this king was outstanding in shrewdness of generalship, in courage, and in brilliance of spirit. But that we may not anticipate his deeds in the preface, we shall proceed to the continuous course of the history, after briefly going back a little in time.

Xerxes, vying with the zeal of the Carthaginians, surpassed them in all his preparations by as much as he exceeded the Carthaginians in the multitude of his peoples. He began to build ships along the whole seacoast subject to his command—Egypt and Phoenicia and Cyprus, and besides these Cilicia and Pamphylia and Pisidia, and further Lycia and Caria and Mysia and the Troad and the cities on the Hellespont and Bithynia and Pontus. And, like the Carthaginians, after preparing for three years he equipped more than twelve hundred warships.

Above all the Athenians, having advanced in glory and courage, became renowned throughout almost the whole inhabited world; for they so increased their leadership that, without the Lacedaemonians and Peloponnesians, by themselves they overcame great Persian forces both by land and by sea, and so humbled the far-famed leadership of the Persians that they compelled them by treaty to liberate all the cities in Asia.

For when Chabrias was archon at Athens, the Romans, instead of consuls, appointed three military tribunes, Lucius Sergius, Marcus Papirius, Marcus Servilius. In their time the Athenians, having voted the war against the Syracusans, refitted the ships and, gathering money, with much zeal prepared everything for the expedition. Having chosen three generals, Alcibiades, Nicias, Lamachus, they appointed them plenipotentiary over all the matters of the war.

For in the archonship of Callimedes at Athens the hundred and fifth Olympiad was held, in which Porus of Cyrene won the foot-race, and the Romans appointed as consuls Gnaeus Genucius and Lucius Aemilius. In their time Philip the son of Amyntas, and father of that Alexander who defeated the Persians, succeeded to the kingdom of the Macedonians for the following reasons.

When Euaenetus was archon at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Lucius Furius and Gaius Manius. In their year Alexander, having succeeded to the kingdom, first dealt out fitting punishment to his father's murderers, and then, having taken all due care for his father's burial, ordered the affairs of his realm far more nobly than anyone had expected.

His father Darius also contributed to this, having before his death made preparations for great forces; for he too, having been defeated by the Athenians at Marathon under the command of Datis, was bitterly disposed toward the victorious Athenians. But Darius, when he was already about to cross against the Greeks, was cut off in the midst of his plans by death, while Xerxes, both because of his father's design and because of the counsel of Mardonius, as has been said, resolved to make war on the Greeks.

But concerning these things we have written the particulars more accurately in two books, this and the one before this; now we shall turn to the deeds before us, having first defined the times suited to the writing.

Of the private citizens, some of those well off in property, wishing to gratify the zeal of the people, constructed triremes of their own, while others undertook to give money for the maintenance of the force; and many of the common citizens and foreigners, and besides the allies, coming voluntarily to the generals, bade them enroll them among the soldiers. Thus all, elated in their hopes, hoped readily to apportion Sicily by lot.

When Amyntas had been defeated by the Illyrians and compelled to pay tribute to his conquerors, the Illyrians took as a hostage Philip, the youngest of his sons, and entrusted him to the Thebans. These in turn entrusted the youth to the father of Epaminondas, and bade him both keep careful watch over the pledge and have charge of his upbringing and education.

For though he was altogether young, and on account of his youth was despised by some, he first won the multitude over to goodwill by appropriate words; for he declared that only the name of king had been changed, and that affairs would be managed in no way worse than under the administration of his father. Then, dealing humanely with the embassies, he urged the Greeks to maintain toward him the goodwill they had inherited from their fathers.

When everything was prepared for the expedition, he ordered his admirals to gather the ships at Cyme and Phocaea; and he himself, having collected the foot and cavalry forces from all the satrapies, advanced from Susa. And when he came to Sardis, he sent heralds into Greece, ordering them to go to all the cities and to demand of the Greeks earth and water.

In the book before this, then, having made the beginning from the expedition of Xerxes, we went through the common deeds down to the year preceding the expedition of the Athenians against Cyprus under the command of Cimon; and in this one, having made the beginning from the expedition of the Athenians against Cyprus, we shall proceed down to the war voted by the Athenians against the Syracusans.

When the fleet was already prepared, it came about that the Hermae throughout the city, being very numerous, were mutilated in a single night. The people, then, thinking that the deed had been done not by chance persons but by those who excelled in reputation, with a view to the overthrow of the democracy, hated wickedness and sought the doers, setting great rewards before the informer.

And since Epaminondas had as his tutor a Pythagorean philosopher, Philip, being brought up along with him, came to share in no small measure in the Pythagorean teachings. And as both pupils brought to their studies natural gifts and love of toil, each proved outstanding in excellence; of whom Epaminondas, having endured great struggles and dangers, beyond all expectation invested his native land with the leadership of Greece, while Philip, using the same beginnings, fell short in no way of the renown of Epaminondas.

He held frequent reviews of the soldiers under arms and trained them in martial exercises, and so made his army obedient. Now he had as a rival for the throne Attalus, the brother of Cleopatra whom Philip had married, and he resolved to remove this man from life; for Cleopatra had in fact borne Philip a child a few days before the king's death.

Dividing his army, he sent off enough men to bridge the Hellespont and to dig through Athos at the neck of the Chersonese, at once making the passage safe and short for his forces, and at the same time hoping by the magnitude of his works to strike the Greeks beforehand with dismay. Those who were sent off for the construction of the works accomplished them quickly because of the multitude of hands at work.

A certain one of the private citizens, coming to the council, said that he had seen some men entering a metic's house at the new moon about midnight, among whom was Alcibiades. Being examined by the council, how, it being night, he recognized the faces, he said that he had seen by the light of the moon. This man, then, having convicted himself of lying, was distrusted, and of the others no one was able to find even a trace of the deed.

For after the death of Amyntas, Alexander, the eldest of his sons, succeeded to the throne. Him Ptolemy of Alorus murdered by treachery and took over the kingdom, and him in turn Perdiccas slew and reigned. But when Perdiccas had been defeated in a great pitched battle by the Illyrians and had fallen in the action, Philip his brother, having escaped from his life as a hostage, took over the kingdom when it was in a wretched state.

Attalus had been sent ahead into Asia as general of the forces along with Parmenion, and being a man of beneficence who cultivated the soldiers in his dealings with them, he enjoyed great favour in the camp. With good reason, then, Alexander was wary of him, lest he should lay claim to the kingship, taking as his allies those of the Greeks who were opposed to Alexander.

The Greeks, when they learned the magnitude of the Persians' force, sent ten thousand hoplites into Thessaly to seize the passes about Tempe. Synetus led the Lacedaemonians, and Themistocles the Athenians. These men, sending ambassadors to the cities, asked them to send soldiers to guard the passes in common; for they were eager to enclose all the Greek cities within the defending lines and to make the war against the Persians a common cause.

A hundred and forty triremes had been prepared, and of the merchant ships and the horse-transports, and besides those carrying the grain and the other supplies, there was a great number; the hoplites and slingers, and besides these the cavalry and the allies, were more than seven thousand apart from those in the crews.

For more than four thousand of the Macedonians had been slain in the battle, and the rest, terrified at the forces of the Illyrians, had become utterly fearful and were dispirited at the prospect of continuing the war.

He therefore chose out one of his friends, Hecataeus, and sent him into Asia with a sufficient body of soldiers, giving him orders, if possible, to bring back Attalus alive, but, if he could not accomplish this, to assassinate the man as quickly as he could.

But since the majority of the Thessalians and of the other Greeks who dwelt near the passes gave earth and water to the messengers who had come from Xerxes, the Greeks, despairing of the guard at Tempe, returned home.

At that time, then, the generals, sitting in council with the council in secret, deliberated how they ought to manage the affairs in Sicily, if they should gain control of the island. It seemed best to them, then, to enslave the Selinuntians and the Syracusans, and on the rest simply to impose tributes, which they should pay each year to the Athenians.

And about the same time the Paeonians, who dwelt near Macedonia, were ravaging the country in contempt of the Macedonians; the Illyrians were gathering great forces and preparing to march into Macedonia; and a certain Pausanias, who had a share in the royal kinship, was attempting, with the help of the king of the Thracians, to come down upon the Macedonian throne. Likewise the Athenians too, being hostile to Philip, were trying to restore Argaeus to the kingdom, and had sent out as general Mantias with three thousand hoplites and a considerable naval force.
So Hecataeus crossed into Asia and, joining Parmenion and Attalus, watched for an opportunity to carry out the action assigned to him.

It is useful to distinguish those of the Greeks who chose the cause of the barbarians, in order that, meeting with reproach, by their disgrace they may deter any who might become traitors to the common freedom.

For when Euthydemus was archon at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Lucius Quintius Cincinnatus and Marcus Fabius Vibulanus. In their time the Athenians, having waged war on behalf of the Egyptians against the Persians and having lost all their ships in the island called Prosopitis, after a short interval resolved to make war again on the Persians on behalf of the Greeks in Asia. Having fitted out a fleet of two hundred triremes and having chosen as general Cimon the son of Miltiades, they ordered him to sail to Cyprus and to make war on the Persians.

On the next day the generals went down with the soldiers to the Piraeus, and all the crowd in the city accompanied them, mingled together of citizens and foreigners, each escorting his own kinsmen and friends.

The Macedonians, because of the disaster in the battle and the magnitude of the dangers bearing down upon them, had fallen into the greatest perplexity. Nevertheless, with such fears and dangers threatening, Philip was not dismayed by the magnitude of the perils expected, but holding the Macedonians together in continual assemblies and urging them on to courage by the power of his eloquence, he made them confident; and improving the military formations and equipping the men properly with their weapons of war, he held continual reviews under arms and competitive exercises.
Alexander, learning that many of the Greeks were eager for revolution, fell into great anxiety.

The Aenianians, then, and the Dolopians and the Malians and the Perrhaebians and the Magnesians ranged themselves with the barbarians even while the guard at Tempe was still in place; and the Achaeans of Phthia and the Locrians and the Thessalians and most of the Boeotians inclined to the barbarians after these had departed.

Cimon, taking up the fleet, equipped with the valor of its men and with lavish supplies, sailed to Cyprus. At that time the generals of the Persian forces were Artabazus and Megabyzus. Artabazus, holding the command, was tarrying in Cyprus, having three hundred triremes, while Megabyzus was encamped about Cilicia, having land forces whose number was three hundred thousand.

The triremes, then, lay at anchor along the whole harbor, adorned with the figureheads on their prows and the brightness of their armor; and the whole circle of the harbor was full of censers and silver mixing-bowls, from which, with golden cups, those who honored the divine poured libations and prayed to succeed in the expedition.
He devised too the close order and equipment of the phalanx, imitating the shield-to-shield array of the heroes at Troy, and was the first to organize the Macedonian phalanx.

For the Athenians, with Demosthenes playing the demagogue against the Macedonians, had heard of Philip's death with delight, and would not yield the leadership of the Greeks to the Macedonians; they sent envoys secretly to Attalus and arranged a common enterprise with him, and urged many of the cities to cling to their freedom.

The Greeks who were sitting in council at the Isthmus voted that those of the Greeks who voluntarily chose the cause of the Persians should be tithed for the gods, should they prevail in the war; and that to those who remained neutral they should send ambassadors to summon them to fight together for the common freedom.

Cimon, having sailed into Cyprus and holding command of the sea, took Citium and Marium by siege, and treated those he subdued humanely. After this, as triremes came against the island from Cilicia and Phoenicia, Cimon, putting out and engaging in battle, sank many of the ships and captured a hundred together with their men, and pursued the rest as far as Phoenicia.

Putting out, then, from the Piraeus, they sailed around the Peloponnese and put in at Corcyra; for there they had been ordered to remain and to take on the neighboring allies. When all had been gathered, they crossed the Ionian strait and put in at the cape of Iapygia, and from there now coasted along Italy.

In his dealings with men he was affable, and through gifts and promises he led the people on to the greatest goodwill, and he contrived shrewdly to counter the multitude of dangers bearing down upon him. For observing that the Athenians were bringing to bear all their ambition upon recovering Amphipolis, and were on that account trying to restore Argaeus to the throne, he withdrew from the city of his own accord, leaving it independent.

The Aetolians voted to restore the exiles from Acarnania who had experienced banishment because of Philip. The Ambraciots, persuaded by Aristarchus, expelled the garrison set over them by Philip and made their city a democracy.

Of these some genuinely chose the alliance, while others put it off for a sufficient time, clinging only to their own safety and watching for the outcome of the war. The Argives, sending ambassadors to the common council, undertook to fight as allies if they were granted some part of the leadership.

The Persians, then, with the surviving ships fled to the land, at the place where Megabyzus was encamped with the land force; and the Athenians, having sailed up and disembarked their soldiers, joined battle, in which Anaxicrates, the other of the generals, having fought brilliantly, ended his life heroically; the rest, having prevailed in the battle and slain many, returned to the ships. After this the Athenians sailed back to Cyprus. These things, then, were done in the first year of the war.

By the Tarentines, then, they were not received, but they sailed past the Metapontines and Heracleotes; and, putting in at Thurii, they met with every kindness. From there, sailing in to Croton and getting a market from the Crotoniates, they sailed past the temple of Lacinian Hera and rounded the cape called Dioscurias.

And sending envoys to the Paeonians, and corrupting some of them with gifts and persuading others with kindly promises, he made an agreement to keep peace with them for the present. Likewise he diverted Pausanias too from his return, persuading with gifts the king who was about to restore him.

Like them the Thebans voted to expel the garrison in the Cadmeia and not to concede to Alexander the leadership of the Greeks. The Arcadians, alone of the Greeks, had neither granted the leadership to Philip nor did they now attend to Alexander.

To these the councilors made plain that, if they thought it more grievous to have a Greek as commander than a barbarian as master, they were right to keep quiet; but if they were ambitious to take the leadership of the Greeks, they said they ought first to have done deeds worthy of it before seeking so great a distinction. After this, when the ambassadors from Xerxes came over Greece and demanded earth and water, all the cities, through their answers, demonstrated their zeal for the common freedom.

After this they passed the place called Scylletium and the Locrians, and, having anchored near Rhegium, tried to persuade the Rhegians to ally with them; but they replied that they would deliberate together with the other Italiotes.

Mantias, the general of the Athenians, having sailed to Methone, himself remained there, but sent Argaeus with the mercenaries against Aegae. He, approaching the city, urged those in Aegae to accept his return and become the leaders of his kingship.

Of the other Peloponnesians, the Argives, the Eleians, the Lacedaemonians, and certain others bestirred themselves toward independence. And of the nations dwelling beyond the borders of Macedonia, not a few were moving toward revolt, and great confusion held the barbarians who lived there.

Xerxes, when he learned that the Hellespont had been bridged and Athos had been dug through, advanced from Sardis, making his march toward the Hellespont; and when he came to Abydus, he led his force across into Europe by the bridge. As he proceeded through Thrace, he took on many soldiers both of the Thracians and of the Greeks bordering on them.

But when no one heeded him, he turned back toward Methone; whereupon Philip, appearing with his soldiers and joining battle, slew many of the mercenaries, and the rest, who had fled for refuge to a certain hill, he let go under a truce, having received from them the surrender of the exiles. Philip, then, having won this his first battle, made the Macedonians more confident for the struggles that lay ahead.

Yet, though affairs of such magnitude and so many terrors beset the kingdom, Alexander, young as he was, settled all the difficulties of his realm with unexpected swiftness. For some he won over by persuasion through personal dealing, some he corrected by fear, and others he mastered by force and made his subjects.

When he came to the place called Doriscus, there he summoned the fleet, so that both forces might be gathered in one place. He also held a review of the whole army; and there were numbered more than eight hundred thousand of the foot, and the warships all together were more than twelve hundred, of which three hundred and twenty were Greek, the Greeks furnishing the crews of men while the king provided the hulls; all the rest were counted as barbarian. Of these the Egyptians furnished two hundred, the Phoenicians three hundred, the Cilicians eighty, the Pamphylians forty, and the Lycians the same number, and besides these the Carians eighty, the Cyprians one hundred and fifty.
While these things were going on, the Thasians colonized the place called Crenides, which later the king, naming it after himself Philippi, filled with settlers.

Of the Greeks, the Dorians who dwell near Caria sent, together with the Rhodians and Coans, forty; the Ionians, with the Chians and Samians, one hundred; the Aeolians, with the Lesbians and Tenedians, forty; the Hellespontines eighty, together with those dwelling about the Pontus; and the islanders fifty—for the king had won over the islands within the Cyaneae and Triopium and Sunium.
Among the historians, Theopompus of Chios, making this the starting-point of his history concerning Philip, wrote fifty-eight books, of which five are missing.

Such, then, was the number of the triremes; the horse-transports were eight hundred and fifty, and the thirty-oared galleys three thousand. So Xerxes was occupied about the review of his forces at Doriscus.

To the councilors of the Greeks, since it had been further reported to them that the forces of the Persians were near, it seemed best quickly to send the naval force to Artemisium in Euboea, seeing that this place was well suited for meeting the enemy, and to Thermopylae enough hoplites to seize beforehand the passes in the narrows and to prevent the barbarians from advancing into Greece; for they were eager to bring within their lines those who had chosen the cause of the Greeks, and to save their allies as far as was possible.

When Pedieus was archon at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Marcus Valerius Lactuca and Spurius Verginius Tricostus. In their time Cimon the general of the Athenians, holding command of the sea, subdued the cities in Cyprus. As there was in Salamis a notable Persian garrison, and the city was full of missiles and arms of all kinds, and besides grain and the other supplies, he judged it advantageous to take it by siege.

The Syracusans, hearing that the forces of the Athenians were at the strait, appointed three plenipotentiary generals, Hermocrates, Sicanus, Heracleides, who enrolled the soldiers and sent ambassadors to the cities in Sicily, begging them to take part in the common safety; for the Athenians, they said, in word were undertaking the war against the Syracusans, but in truth wished to subdue the whole island.

In the archonship of Eucharistus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Quintus Servilius and Quintus Genucius. In their time Philip, having sent envoys to Athens, persuaded the people to make peace with him, since he no longer laid claim to Amphipolis.

First he reminded the Thessalians of their ancient kinship through Heracles, and, raising their hopes with humane words and great promises besides, he persuaded them by a common decree of Thessaly to grant him the leadership they had inherited from his father.

Eurybiades the Lacedaemonian was in command of the whole fleet, and Leonidas the king of the Spartiates of the men sent to Thermopylae—a man who took great pride in his courage and generalship. He, on receiving the authority, gave orders for only a thousand men to accompany him on the expedition.

For thus he supposed he would most easily gain control of all Cyprus and would dismay the Persians, who were unable to come to the aid of the Salaminians because the Athenians held command of the sea, but, by abandoning their allies, would be held in contempt, and in general that the whole war would be decided by all Cyprus being subdued by force; which indeed came to pass.

The Acragantines, then, and the Naxians said they would ally with the Athenians, while the Camarinaeans and Messenians agreed to keep the peace but deferred their answers about the alliance; the Himeraeans and Selinuntians, and besides these the Geloans and Catanaeans, undertook to fight together with the Syracusans. The cities of the Sicels inclined in goodwill toward the Syracusans, but nevertheless, remaining quiet, awaited the outcome.

And having been freed from the war with the Athenians, and learning that Agis the king of the Paeonians had died, he supposed that he had an opportunity to attack the Paeonians. Marching therefore into Paeonia and defeating the barbarians in a pitched battle, he compelled the nation to obey the Macedonians.

After them he won over to a like goodwill the neighbouring nations, and advanced to Pylae; and, having convened the council of the Amphictyons, he persuaded them to grant him by a common decree the leadership of the Greeks.

When the ephors said that he was leading a very few against a great force, and ordered him to take more, he said to them in secret that for preventing the barbarians from passing through the narrows the few were enough, but for the deed on which they were now setting out, the many were too few.

For the Athenians, having established a siege about Salamis, made assaults each day, and the soldiers in the city, having missiles and supplies, easily defended themselves from the walls against the besiegers.

As the Egestaeans did not agree to give more than thirty talents, the generals of the Athenians, accusing them, put out from Rhegium with the force and put in at Naxos in Sicily. Those in the city having received them kindly, they sailed from there to Catana.

And since the Illyrians remained as enemies, he was eager to subdue these also. Straightway, then, gathering an assembly and exhorting the soldiers with fitting words to the war, he marched into the country of the Illyrians, having no fewer than ten thousand foot and six hundred horse.
To the Ambraciots, who sent envoys to him, he spoke humanely and persuaded them that they had but slightly anticipated the independence which he was about to grant them gladly of his own accord.

As this answer was riddling and obscure, they asked him whether he intended to lead them on some trivial enterprise. He replied that in word he was leading them to the defense of the passes, but in deed to die for the common freedom; so that, if the thousand should go, Sparta would be the more illustrious when they had perished, but if the Lacedaemonians should march out in full force, Lacedaemon would be utterly destroyed; for none of them would dare to flee in order to obtain safety.

Artaxerxes the king, learning of the reverses about Cyprus and having deliberated with his friends about the war, judged it advantageous to make peace with the Greeks. He wrote, therefore, to the commanders and satraps about Cyprus, on what terms they might be able to come to a settlement with the Greeks.
As the Catanaeans did not receive the soldiers into the city but allowed the generals to enter and granted them an assembly, the generals of the Athenians discussed the alliance.

Bardylis, the king of the Illyrians, learning of the enemy's approach, at first sent envoys about a settlement, on the terms that both parties should be masters of the cities they then controlled; but when Philip declared that he desired peace, but would not however grant it unless the Illyrians withdrew from all the Macedonian cities, the envoys returned without success, and Bardylis, trusting in his previous victories and in the valour of the Illyrians, advanced against the enemy with his force; he had ten thousand picked foot and about five hundred horse.

To overawe those who would not obey, he led the army of the Macedonians, arrayed in a manner to inspire terror. Using rapid marches, he came into Boeotia, and, encamping near the Cadmeia, struck great fear into the city of the Thebans.
Of the Lacedaemonians, then, there were a thousand, and with them three hundred Spartiates; and of the other Greeks who were sent out together with them to Thermopylae, three thousand.

Therefore Artabazus and Megabyzus sent ambassadors to Athens to discuss a settlement. The Athenians, consenting, and having sent plenipotentiary ambassadors, of whom Callias the son of Hipponicus was the leader, there were made treaties of peace for the Athenians and their allies with the Persians, of which the chief points are these: that all the Greek cities in Asia be autonomous; that the satraps of the Persians not come down to the sea closer than a three days' journey, nor a warship sail within Phaselis and the Cyaneae; and, these things being fulfilled by the king and the generals, that the Athenians not campaign into the country which the king rules.

As Alcibiades was addressing the assembly, some of the soldiers, having broken open a postern gate, burst into the city; for which reason the Catanaeans were compelled to take part in the war against the Syracusans.

When the armies drew near to one another and clashed in battle with a great shout, Philip, holding the right wing with the best of the Macedonians fighting at his side, ordered the cavalry to ride round and attack the barbarians on the flank, while he himself, falling upon the enemy front to front, joined in a fierce battle.

At this very time the Athenians, learning of the king's passage into Boeotia, abandoned their former contempt; for the swiftness of the young man and the energy of his actions greatly alarmed those who were ill-disposed toward him.

So Leonidas advanced with four thousand toward Thermopylae. The Locrians who dwelt near the passes had given earth and water to the Persians and had undertaken to seize the passes beforehand; but when they learned that Leonidas had come to Thermopylae, they changed their minds and went over to the Greeks.

The treaties having been completed, the Athenians led their forces away from Cyprus, having won a brilliant victory and made most distinguished treaties. It came to pass also that Cimon, while tarrying about Cyprus, died of disease.

The Illyrians, forming themselves into a square, stoutly maintained the struggle. And at first for a long time the battle was evenly balanced, owing to the surpassing valour on both sides, and as many were slain and still more wounded, the fortune of the conflict inclined now this way, now that, ever swaying with the prowess of the combatants; but afterward, as the cavalry pressed hard from the flank and the rear, and Philip with the bravest fought heroically, the mass of the Illyrians was forced to take to flight.

The Athenians therefore voted to bring in their property from the countryside and to take all possible care of the walls. To Alexander they sent envoys, asking him to pardon them for being slow to concede the leadership.

There came to Thermopylae also a thousand Locrians and as many Malians, and Phocians not much short of a thousand, and likewise about four hundred Thebans from the other faction; for the inhabitants of Thebes were at variance among themselves about the alliance with the Persians. The Greeks who were marshaled with Leonidas, being such in number, remained about Thermopylae, awaiting the arrival of the Persians.

The pursuit having extended over a great distance and many having been slain in the flight, Philip, recalling the Macedonians with the trumpet and setting up a trophy, buried his own dead; while the Illyrians, sending envoys and withdrawing from all the Macedonian cities, obtained peace. There were slain of the Illyrians in this battle more than seven thousand.

Among the envoys sent out was Demosthenes; but he did not go with the rest to meet Alexander, and turned back from Cithaeron to Athens, either because he feared on account of his policies against the Macedonians, or because he wished to keep himself blameless toward the king of the Persians.

For they say that he had received much money from the Persians in order to conduct his policy against the Macedonians; concerning which, they say, Aeschines too, reproaching Demosthenes with his bribery in one of his speeches, said: “For the present, indeed, the royal gold has flooded over his extravagance; yet not even this will be enough, for no wealth has ever yet got the better of a base character.”

Alexander, giving the Athenian envoys humane replies, freed the people from their great fear. Then, having sent word to the embassies and the deputies to meet at Corinth, when those who were accustomed to sit in council had assembled, the king addressed them; and, using reasonable words, he persuaded the Greeks to vote Alexander general with full powers of Greece, and to join him in the campaign against the Persians for the wrongs they had done to the Greeks. Having obtained this honour, the king returned with his army to Macedonia.

Xerxes, after the review of his forces, advanced with the whole army; and as far as the city of Acanthus the whole fleet sailed alongside his foot-army as it marched, but from there they were carried over by the place that had been dug through into the other sea, quickly and safely.

When Philiscus was archon at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Titus Romilius Vaticanus and Gaius Veturius Cichorius, and the Eleans celebrated the eighty-third Olympiad, in which Crison of Himera won the stadium-race.

While these things were being done, those at Athens who hated Alcibiades because of their private enmity, having as a pretext the mutilation of the statues, slandered him in their public speeches as having made a conspiracy against the people. There contributed to their slanders what had been done among the Argives; for the personal guest-friends who had agreed to overthrow the democracy in Argos were all put to death by the citizens.

At the same time as these things were being done, the Lacedaemonians resolved to campaign against Mantinea, taking no thought of the treaties that had been made, for the following causes. There being already among the Greeks the common peace of Antalcidas, by which all the cities had got rid of their garrisons and received their independence by agreement, the Lacedaemonians, being by nature lovers of rule and warlike in their inclinations, did not endure the peace as a heavy burden, and longing for the dominion of Greece they had formerly held, were excited in their impulses toward revolution. 5.2. Immediately, then, they threw the cities into disorder and through their own friends contrived factions in them, of which some furnished plausible occasions to them for the disturbance. For having recovered their independence, they demanded an account from those who had presided over them during the leadership of the Lacedaemonians; and the reckonings being bitter because the peoples bore malice, and many being banished, they declared themselves helpers of those who were being put down by faction. 5.3. Receiving these and sending them out with a force for their returns, they enslaved first the weaker cities, and after this subduing the more notable ones too they made them subject, not even keeping the common treaties two years. Seeing that the city of the Mantineans was a neighbour and full of valiant men, they suspected its increase that came from the peace, and were eager to humble the spirits of the men. 5.4. Therefore at first, sending envoys to Mantinea, they ordered them to tear down their walls and themselves to remove, all of them, into the ancient five villages, out of which they had originally united into Mantinea. No one heeding them, they sent out a force and besieged the city. 5.5. The Mantineans, sending envoys to Athens, asked them to help them. The Athenians not choosing to transgress the common treaties, nevertheless by themselves the Mantineans, withstanding the siege, vigorously defended themselves against the enemy. And the affairs of Greece in this manner took the beginning of new wars. 6.1. In Sicily Dionysius the tyrant of the Syracusans, being released from the wars against the Carthaginians, had much peace and leisure. Therefore he undertook to write poems with much eagerness, and he sent for those who had a reputation in these, and honouring them above others he spent his time with them and had them as overseers and correctors of his poems. Being lifted up by these, because of his benefactions, with flattering speeches, he boasted much more over his poems than over his successes in war. 6.2. Of the poets who were with him, Philoxenus the dithyrambic poet, who had the greatest reputation for the composition of his own poetry, at the symposium, when the poems of the tyrant, being wretched, had been read, was asked what judgement he had concerning the poems. He answering rather frankly, the tyrant, taking offence at what was said, and blaming him that out of envy he had spoken slander, ordered the servants at once to lead him off to the quarries. 6.3. On the next day, the friends urging him to give pardon to Philoxenus, being reconciled with him he again took the same men to the symposium. As the drinking advanced, and again Dionysius boasted about his own poems, and brought forward certain verses of those that seemed successful, and asked, "What sort do the poems appear to you to be?"—he said nothing else, but calling the servants of Dionysius, ordered them to lead him off to the quarries. 6.4. At that time, then, on account of the wit of his words, Dionysius, smiling, bore the frankness, the laughter blunting the censure; but a little later, when both his acquaintances and Dionysius were deprecating the ill-timed frankness, Philoxenus made a paradoxical promise. For he said that by his answer he would preserve at once both the truth and the satisfaction of Dionysius; and he was not false to it. 6.5. For when the tyrant brought forward certain verses containing pitiable sufferings, and asked, "What sort do the poems appear?"—he said, "Pitiful," preserving both meanings through the ambiguity. For Dionysius took "pitiful" to mean piteous and full of compassion, and that such things are the achievements of good poets, whence he received him as having praised him; but the others, taking the true meaning, understood that "pitiful" was said as describing the nature of a failure. 7.1. Something similar happened also in the case of Plato the philosopher. For having sent for this man, at first he deemed him worthy of the greatest acceptance, seeing that he had a frankness worthy of philosophy; but later, taking offence at him over certain discourses, he became wholly estranged, and leading him to the market sold him as a slave for twenty minas. But the philosophers, coming together, bought him out and sent him to Greece, adding the friendly admonition that the wise man should associate with tyrants either as little as possible or as agreeably as possible. 7.2. Dionysius, not desisting from his eagerness for poetry, sent to the Olympic festival the most fine-voiced of the actors to perform his poems among the crowds with song. These at first, because of their fine voices, struck the hearers with amazement, but after this, when reflection set in, they were despised and carried off much laughter. 7.3. Dionysius, hearing of the contempt for his poems, fell into excessive grief; and the affliction ever taking on increase, a maddened disposition seized his soul, and saying that all his friends envied him, he suspected them as plotting. And at last he proceeded to such a pitch of frenzy and derangement that of his friends many he slew on false charges, and not a few he banished; among whom were Philistus and Leptines his brother, men distinguished in valour and who had rendered him many and great services in the wars. 7.4. These, then, fleeing to Thurii in Italy and meeting with great acceptance among the Italiotes, later, at the request of Dionysius, were reconciled, and returning to Syracuse were restored to their former goodwill; and Leptines married the daughter of Dionysius. These things, then, were done in this year.

Now that we have gone through the affairs of Macedonia and Illyria, we shall pass over to events of another kind. For in Sicily Dionysius the younger, tyrant of the Syracusans, having succeeded to the dominion in earlier times, but being inactive and far inferior to his father, pretended, because of his inactivity, to be peaceable and gentle in his character.

Now that we have gone through the affairs of Greece, we shall transfer our account to the events in Asia. After the death of Philip, Attalus at first attempted to stir up revolt and arranged with the Athenians a common enterprise against Alexander; but afterward, changing his mind, he kept the letter that had been delivered to him from Demosthenes and sent it to Alexander, and with humane words tried to clear away the slanders against himself.

When he came to the Malian Gulf, he learned that the enemy had occupied the passes beforehand. Therefore there he reinforced his army by summoning his allies from Europe, who fell little short of two hundred thousand, so that he had in all not fewer than a million, apart from the naval force.

In their time the Megarians revolted from the Athenians, and, sending an embassy to the Lacedaemonians, made an alliance; the Athenians, provoked, sent soldiers into the country of the Megarians, and, having plundered the possessions, became masters of much booty. As those from the city came to the aid of the country, a battle took place, in which the Athenians, having conquered, pursued the Megarians together within their walls.

The people, then, trusting the accusations and being terribly provoked by the demagogues, sent the Salaminian ship to Sicily, ordering Alcibiades to come as quickly as possible for the trial. The ship having arrived at Catana, Alcibiades, hearing from the ambassadors what had been decided by the people, took up those who had been slandered with him into his own trireme and sailed out together with the Salaminian.

For this reason, having taken over the war against the Carthaginians, he made peace with them; and likewise, having warred sluggishly for some time against the Lucanians, and having gained the advantage in the last battles, he gladly ended the war with them.

But when Hecataeus, in accordance with the king's orders, had assassinated Attalus, the Macedonian forces in Asia ceased to be stirred toward revolt, since Attalus had been slain and Parmenion was most intimately disposed toward Alexander.

The whole multitude of those in the warships and of those bringing the provisions and the rest of the supplies was not less than the aforesaid; so that it is no wonder what is said about the multitude of the men gathered by Xerxes; for they say that the ever-flowing rivers failed because of the continuous mass, and that the seas were hidden by the sails of the ships. Thus the greatest forces of all that are handed down to historical memory are recorded as those that were with Xerxes.

In Sicily Dionysius the tyrant of the Sicilians, since he had made peace with the Carthaginians, set his mind rather upon the security of his tyranny; for he supposed that the Syracusans, being released from the war, would have leisure to recover their freedom. 7.2. Observing that the Island of the city was very strong and could easily be guarded, he walled this off from the rest of the city with a costly wall, and built into it high and close-set towers, and before it market-buildings and porticoes able to receive a multitude of people. 7.3. He built within it also a citadel costly and fortified for sudden refuges, and enclosed within its wall the dockyards by the little harbour called Laccius; these dockyards, holding sixty triremes, had a gate that could be shut, through which the ships sailed in one at a time. 7.4. Of the land he picked out the best and bestowed it upon his friends and upon those appointed to commands, while the rest he divided equally between foreigner and citizen, including under the name of citizens the freed slaves, whom he called neo-politai. 7.5. He distributed the houses also among the multitude, except those on the Island; these he gave to his friends and to the mercenaries. And when he thought he had arranged the affairs of his tyranny well, he led his force out against the Sicels, eager to bring all the independent peoples under himself, but most of all these, because they had earlier been allied with the Carthaginians. 7.6. He, then, marching against the city of the Herbessini, made preparations for the siege. But the Syracusans serving with him, being in control of their arms, formed combinations and accused one another, because they had not joined the cavalry in the overthrow of the tyrant. The commander appointed by Dionysius over the soldiers at first threatened one of those speaking freely, and when that man answered back boldly, came on as though to strike him. 7.7. Provoked at this, the soldiers killed the prefect, Doricus by name, and crying to the citizens to win freedom, they sent for the cavalry from Aetna; for these, having been driven out at the beginning of the tyranny, were dwelling in that stronghold. 8.1. Dionysius, struck with dismay at the revolt of the Syracusans, broke off the siege and hastened to Syracuse, eager to seize the city. When he had fled away, those who had made the revolt chose as generals the men who had killed the prefect, and taking the cavalry from Aetna encamped against the tyrant in the place called Epipolae, and shut him off from his exit into the countryside. 8.2. Immediately too they sent envoys to the Messenians and the Rhegians, asking them to help by sea in the cause of freedom; for these cities were accustomed at that time to man no fewer than eighty triremes. These the cities then dispatched to the Syracusans, eager to share in the cause of freedom. 8.3. They proclaimed also a sum of money to those who should slay the tyrant, and promised those of the mercenaries who came over a share in the citizenship. They constructed also engines, with which by shaking the walls they would breach them, and they assaulted the Island day by day, and received humanely those of the mercenaries who came over. 8.4. Dionysius, shut off from his exit into the country and being abandoned by the mercenaries, gathered his friends to take counsel about the present circumstances; for the affairs of his dominion were so utterly despaired of that he no longer sought how he might subdue the Syracusans, but what kind of death he might endure so as not to make the dissolution of his rule wholly inglorious. 8.5. Heloris then, one of his friends—or, as some say, his adopted father—said to him that the tyranny was a fine winding-sheet; while Polyxenus the brother-in-law declared that he ought to take the swiftest horse and ride into the territory of the Carthaginians to the Campanians; for Himilcon had left these behind to guard the regions in Sicily. But Philistus, who afterward composed the histories, contradicting Polyxenus, said that it was fitting not to gallop out of the tyranny on a running horse, but to be dragged out by the leg. 8.6. Heeding him, Dionysius decided to endure anything rather than abandon his rule willingly. Therefore, sending envoys to the rebels, he begged them to grant him leave to depart from the city with his own people, while privately he sent word to the Campanians and agreed to give them whatever money they should ask for the relief of the siege. 9.1. Having quickly accomplished the journey, they appeared unexpectedly to the Syracusans, and slaying many of them forced their way through to Dionysius. There sailed in also three hundred mercenaries to the tyrant at the same time, so that he revived in his hopes. 9.4. In this year Evagoras the king of the Salaminians came to Cyprus from Egypt, conveying money from Acoris the king of Egypt, less than had been expected. Finding Salamis vigorously besieged and being abandoned by his allies, he was compelled to send an embassy about a settlement. 8.2. Tiribazus, who had the command of the whole, said that he would agree to the settlement if Evagoras would withdraw from all the cities in Cyprus, and, reigning over Salamis alone, would pay to the King of the Persians a fixed tribute each year and do what was commanded, as a slave to a master. 8.3. Evagoras, although the terms were heavy, agreed to all the rest, but objected to doing what was commanded as a slave to a master, and said that he ought to be subject as a king to a king. Tiribazus not agreeing, Orontes the other general, envying the reputation of Tiribazus, sent letters secretly to Artaxerxes against Tiribazus. 8.4. He accused him, first, that, being able to take Salamis, he did not accomplish this, but received an embassy from Evagoras and conferred about a common undertaking; and likewise that he was privately making an alliance with the Lacedaemonians, being a friend of theirs; and that he had sent certain men to Delphi to ask the god about a rising; and the greatest thing, that he was making the commanders of the forces his own by goodwill, winning them over by honours and gifts and besides by promises. 8.5. The King, reading the letter and trusting the slanders, wrote to Orontes to arrest Tiribazus and send him to himself. He doing what was commanded, Tiribazus, brought up to the King and demanding to obtain a trial, was for the present given over to prison, but after this, the King having a war against the Cadusii and putting off the trial, the matters of the tribunal were dragged out. 9.1. Orontes, succeeding to the command of the forces in Cyprus, and seeing Evagoras again confidently enduring the siege, and besides this the soldiers ill enduring the arrest of Tiribazus, and on this account disobeying and abandoning the siege, Orontes, fearing the strangeness of the situation, sent to Evagoras men to confer about the settlement and to bid him conclude the peace on the terms on which he had thought fit to agree with Tiribazus. 9.2. Evagoras, then, unexpectedly escaped the capture, and concluded the peace, so as to reign over Salamis and to give the fixed tribute each year and to obey, as a king a king who commanded. The Cyprian War, then, which had lasted almost ten years, and most of the time had been occupied with preparations, having for two years at the end been continuously fought, was dissolved in this manner. 9.3. Glos, who had the admiralship of the fleet, having married the daughter of Tiribazus, being greatly afraid lest, seeming to have cooperated with Tiribazus in the affair, he should meet with punishment from the King, resolved by a new undertaking of affairs to secure his own position. Being well supplied with money and soldiers, and besides having made the trierarchs his own by goodwill, he resolved to revolt from the King. 9.4. Immediately, then, sending an embassy to Acoris the king of the Egyptians, he made an alliance against the King, and writing to the Lacedaemonians he stirred them up against the King, and promised to give a quantity of money and made the other great promises, undertaking to assist them in their affairs in Greece and to help them recover their ancestral leadership. 9.5. The Spartans had long since resolved to recover their leadership, and were now already throwing the cities into disorder and were manifest to all as enslaving the cities. Besides this, being in ill repute for seeming, in the agreement with the King, to have given up the Greeks in Asia, they repented of what had been done and sought a plausible pretext for the war against Artaxerxes. Therefore they gladly concluded the alliance with Glos. 10.1. Artaxerxes, having ended the war against the Cadusii, set up the trial for Tiribazus, and appointed three judges of those most esteemed among the Persians. About these times other judges, seeming to have judged badly, were flayed alive, and over the judicial seats the skins being stretched, upon these the judges gave judgement, having before their eyes an example of the penalty for judging badly. 10.2. The accusers, then, reading the letter sent by Orontes, said that this was sufficient for accusation; but Tiribazus, against the slander concerning Evagoras, brought forward the agreement made by Orontes that Evagoras should obey the King as a king a king, while he himself had concluded the peace so that Evagoras should obey the King as a slave a master; and concerning the oracles he said that the god gives no responses at all about death, and of this he produced as witnesses all the Greeks who were present.
