After this he both took the citadel by siege and, bringing over the city Crannon, agreed to give back the cities to the Thessalians; but despising the engagement, and bringing in considerable garrisons, he himself held the cities. The Pheraean Alexander, both pursued and struck with dismay, returned to Pherae. And the affairs in Thessaly were in this state. 62.1. In the Peloponnese the Lacedaemonians sent Polytropus as general into Arcadia, having a thousand citizen hoplites and five hundred exiles of the Argives and Boeotians. He, coming to Arcadian Orchomenus, guarded this city, which was favourably disposed toward the Spartans. 62.2. Lycomedes the Mantinean, being general of the Arcadians, taking the men called the chosen, being five thousand, came to Orchomenus. The Lacedaemonians leading the force out of the city, a fierce battle took place, in which both the general of the Lacedaemonians was slain and of the others about two hundred; the rest were pursued together into the city. 62.3. The Arcadians, although they had conquered, nevertheless were on their guard against the weight of Sparta, and did not suppose they would be able by themselves to fight the war against the Lacedaemonians. Therefore, taking on the Argives and Eleians, at first they sent envoys to Athens, asking them to make an alliance against the Spartans; but when no one heeded them, sending an embassy to the Thebans they persuaded them to conclude an alliance against the Lacedaemonians. 62.4. Immediately, then, the Boeotians led out the force, taking on as allies both Locrians and Phocians. These, then, advanced against the Peloponnese, Epaminondas and Pelopidas being boeotarchs; for to these the other boeotarchs had willingly yielded the generalship, because of the understanding and valour of the men. 62.5. When they came to Arcadia, there came to them in full force both the Arcadians and Eleians and Argives and all the other allies. More than fifty thousand being gathered, their leaders, taking counsel together, resolved to march against Sparta itself and to ravage all Laconia.

We think it just first to record the punishment that came from the gods upon those who transgressed against the oracle; for in general not only upon the perpetrators of the sacrilege, but also upon all who merely touched the lawlessness, an inexorable vengeance followed from the divine power.

Darius, excelling in generalship and having the quantity of the dust as an ally, made his withdrawal unlike that of the other barbarians; for, rushing off in the opposite direction and having his own withdrawal hidden by the rising dust, he himself escaped without danger and brought all who were with him safely to the villages lying behind the Macedonians.

The barbarians, as the fleet was just sailing up, deceived by the Persian ships and equipment, supposed them to be their own triremes. Therefore these received the Athenians as being friends, while Cimon, when night had now come on, having disembarked his soldiers, and being received as a friend by them, fell upon the encampment of the barbarians.

Therefore they sailed against Pylos with forty-five well-fitted triremes, and campaigned with twelve thousand foot, thinking it disgraceful that those who had not dared to come to the aid of Attica when it was being ravaged should fortify and seize a place in the Peloponnese.

A report was spread also throughout the city that the Syracusans in full force with the allies were marching to aid the Himeraeans, and that Hannibal was about to fill the triremes at Motya with the strongest men and, sailing around to Syracuse, to seize the city, empty of its defenders.

For the architect of the seizure of the temple, Philomelus, in a certain warlike circumstance, cast himself down; and his brother Onomarchus, succeeding to the command of the desperate men, with the Phocians and mercenaries who fought beside him in Thessaly, was cut down and crucified.
At last all the barbarians having taken to flight, and the Macedonians always killing the hindmost, soon all the ground near the plain was filled with corpses.

As great confusion arose among the Persians, Cimon and his men slew all whom they met, and, having caught in his tent the other general of the barbarians, Pherendates, the nephew of the king, slew him; and of the rest, some they killed, others they wounded, and all, because of the unexpectedness of the attack, they forced to flee; and in general such consternation and ignorance held the Persians that the greater part did not know who those attacking them were.

These, then, Thrasymedes being in command, encamped near Pylos. An impulse having fallen upon the multitude to endure every danger and to subdue Pylos by force, they stationed the ships prow-foremost at the mouth of the harbor, in order through these to block the entrance of the enemy, and by land, attacking the wall by relays and bringing the greatest ambition, they put up marvelous struggles.
Therefore Diocles the general of those in Himera advised the admirals to sail out to Syracuse as quickly as possible, lest the city be taken by storm, the strongest men being absent in the battle.

The third, Phayllus, who cut up most of the offerings, being sick of a long disease, could not even be quickly released from his punishment. And last of all Phalaecus, taking up the remnants of the sacrilege, lived for a considerable time in wanderings and great fears and dangers, not in order that he might become more blessed than those who had been impious with him, but in order that, being tortured for a longer time and becoming, through his misfortune, known to many, he might have a calamity that was talked of everywhere.

And so of the barbarians there were cut down in this battle, horse and foot together, more than ninety thousand; of the Macedonians about five hundred were slain, and the wounded were very many, among whom were also the most distinguished of the commanders: Hephaestion, the leader of the bodyguards, was wounded, struck in the arm with a lance; and of the generals Perdiccas and Coenus, and besides Menidas and certain others of the distinguished commanders. Such, then, was the end of the pitched battle at Arbela.

For they did not suppose that the Greeks had come against them with a force, being persuaded that they had no land army at all; but the Pisidians, who were neighbors and hostilely disposed toward them, they supposed had come with a force. Therefore, thinking that the onset of the enemy was from the mainland, they fled to the ships as to friends.

To the island called Sphacteria, which extends lengthwise and makes the harbor calm, they ferried the best of the Lacedaemonians and the allies. This they did, wishing to anticipate the Athenians in seizing the island, which lay very conveniently for the siege.

Therefore it seemed advantageous to them to abandon the city, and to embark half on the triremes—for these would convey them until they got outside the Himeraean territory—while with the other half they would keep watch until the triremes should return again.

For he, after his flight according to the agreement, at first tarried with the mercenaries about the Peloponnese, holding the soldiers together out of the remnants of the temple-plunder, and after this, hiring at Corinth large freight ships and having four light galleys, he prepared for the voyage to Italy and Sicily, thinking that in these regions he would either seize some city or obtain mercenary service; for there happened to be a war between the Lucanians and the Tarentines. And to those sailing with him he said that he was sailing by summons from those in Italy and Sicily.
As the night was moonless and dark, it came about that the ignorance was much increased and no one could see the truth.

Spending the whole day in the assaults on the wall and being wounded because of the superior height of the wall, they did not cease from their force; therefore many of them died, and not a few were wounded, forcing their way against a fortified place.

The Himeraeans being indignant at what was said, but having nothing else to do, the triremes were manned by night in haste, mingled together with women and children and the other persons, who sailed off on these as toward Messene;

Therefore, much slaughter taking place because of the disorder of the barbarians, Cimon, having told his soldiers beforehand to run together to the beacon that would be raised, raised the signal by the ships, being wary lest, the soldiers being scattered and rushing to plunder, something unexpected might happen.

The Athenians, having previously seized a place strong also by nature, and having a quantity of missiles and much abundance of the other useful things, defended zealously; for they hoped that, prevailing in the undertaking, they would bring the whole war into the Peloponnese and would ravage the country of the enemy piece by piece.

and Diocles, taking his own soldiers and leaving behind those who had fallen in the battle, set out, making the journey homeward. Many of the Himeraeans with their children and wives set out with Diocles, since the triremes could not hold the crowd.

When all had gathered to the beacon and ceased from plunder, then they withdrew to the ships, and on the next day, setting up a trophy, they sailed off to Cyprus, having won two fairest victories, the one by land, the other by sea; for never yet are such and so great deeds recorded as having taken place on the same day with both naval and land forces.

Cimon, having through his own generalship and valor achieved great things, won a far-famed glory not only among the citizens, but also among the other Greeks. For he had taken three hundred and forty ships, and more than twenty thousand men, and a notable quantity of money.

As the siege had unsurpassable zeal on both sides, and the Spartiates were bringing force against the walls, many others were admired for their deeds of valor, but Brasidas met with the greatest acceptance.

Those left behind in the city passed the night under arms on the walls; and at daybreak, the Carthaginians having encamped about the city and made frequent assaults, the Himeraeans who were left fought unsparingly, awaiting the arrival of the ships.

When he had sailed out and was on the open sea, certain of the soldiers conveyed in the largest ship, in which Phalaecus himself sailed, fell to talking with one another, suspecting that no one had summoned them; for they neither saw commanders from those who summoned them sailing with them, nor was the voyage a short one, but a long and difficult one lay before them.

When Aristophon was archon at Athens, in Rome Gaius Domitius and Aulus Cornelius succeeded to the consulship. In their time, the battle at Arbela having been reported in Greece, many of the cities, looking with suspicion on the growth of the Macedonians, resolved to cling to their freedom while the affairs of the Persians still held out;

The Persians, having fallen into such great defeats, built still more triremes, fearing the growth of the Athenians. For from these times the city of the Athenians received much increase, being equipped with a quantity of money and having met with great glory in courage and generalship.

For when the trierarchs did not dare to bring the triremes to the land because of the difficulty of the places, Brasidas, being a trierarch, shouted and exhorted the helmsman not to spare the ship, but even by force to bring the trireme to the land; for it was disgraceful for the Spartiates to be unsparing of their life for the sake of victory, but to spare the ships and look on at the Athenians holding command of Laconia.

That day, then, they held out, but on the next, the triremes now appearing, it came about that the wall fell under the engines, and the Iberians burst into the city in a mass. Some of the barbarians defended themselves against the Himeraeans coming to the aid, others, having seized the walls, received their own men.

Wherefore, distrusting what was said and fearing the overseas campaign, they banded together, and especially those of the mercenaries who held commands. At last, drawing their swords and striking terror into both Phalaecus and the helmsman, they compelled them to sail back again. The same thing being done also by those conveyed in the other ships, they sailed back to the Peloponnese.

for they thought that Darius would help them and would supply a quantity of money, so that they would be able to gather great mercenary forces, and that Alexander would not be able to divide his forces.

The people of the Athenians, setting aside a tithe from the spoils, dedicated it to the god, and inscribed this on the dedicated offering they had made: Since the sea divided Europe from Asia and impetuous Ares holds the cities of mortals, never yet did such a deed of earthly men take place at once on the mainland and on the sea. For these men, having destroyed many Medes in Cyprus, took at sea a hundred Phoenician ships full of men; and greatly groaned Asia, smitten by them with both hands in the might of war.

Finally, having compelled the helmsman to bring the ship in, the trireme ran aground, and Brasidas, mounting on the gangway of the ship, from it defended himself against the multitude of Athenians who ran together against him. And at first he slew many of those approaching, but afterward, as many missiles bore upon him, he was struck by many wounds in front.

The city, then, having been taken by storm, for a long time the barbarians killed all whom they caught without compassion. When Hannibal ordered them to take alive, the slaughter ceased, but the wealth in the houses was plundered.

Gathering at the promontory Malea of Laconia, they found there Cnossian envoys who had sailed from Crete to gather mercenaries; and when these had conferred with Phalaecus and the commanders and given them considerable pay, they all sailed off with them. Putting in at Cnossus in Crete, they straightway, at the first onset, seized the city called Lyctus.
But if they looked on while the Persians were utterly defeated, the Greeks would be left isolated and would no longer be able to take thought for their own freedom.

Finally, much blood having been shed through the wounds, and because of this having fainted, his arm fell forward out of the ship, and his shield, slipping off and falling into the sea, fell into the hands of the enemy.

Hannibal, having plundered the temples and dragged off the suppliants who had fled to them, burned them, and razed the city to the ground, which had been inhabited two hundred and forty years; and of the captives, having distributed the women and children to the army, he kept them under guard, but the men captured, being about three thousand, he led to the place where formerly Hamilcar his grandfather had been killed by Gelon, and, having tortured them all, he slaughtered them.

To the Lyctians, who had been driven from their native city, an unexpected and swift help appeared. For about the same time, the Tarentines being at war with the Lucanians and with the Lacedaemonians, their ancestors, and having sent envoys about help, the Spartans, through their kinship, being eager to ally themselves, quickly gathered a land and naval force, and appointed as general of it Archidamus the king; and as they were about to set out for Italy, the Lyctians asked them first to help them; and the Lacedaemonians, persuaded and sailing to Crete, defeated the mercenaries and saved for the Lyctians their native city.
The revolution that took place in Thrace at this same time also invited the Greeks to revolt;

After this he, having heaped up many corpses of the enemy, was himself carried half-dead from the ship by his own men, so far surpassing the others in courage that, whereas the others who lost their shield were punished with death, he, on the same charge, won glory.

After this, having disbanded the army, he sent the allies from Sicily to their native lands, with whom the Campanians too went, accusing the Carthaginians of having been the chief causes of the successes but of having received unworthy thanks for their deeds;

for Memnon, who had been appointed general of Thrace, having a force and being full of spirit, stirred up the barbarians, and, becoming a rebel against Alexander and quickly gaining control of a great force, openly declared himself for war.

The Lacedaemonians, then, making continuous assaults on Pylos and having lost many soldiers, remained vigorously amid the dangers. One might marvel at the paradox of fortune and the peculiarity of the disposition of affairs about Pylos.

and Hannibal, having put aboard the warships and cargo ships the force, and leaving behind enough soldiers for the allies, sailed out of Sicily. When he put in to Carthage with much booty, all met him, welcoming and honoring him as having accomplished in a short time greater things than the former generals.

Therefore Antipater, taking up his whole force, advanced through Macedonia into Thrace and waged war against Memnon. While he was engaged in this, the Lacedaemonians, supposing that they had an opportunity to prepare for war, urged the Greeks to unite in purpose for their freedom.

For the Athenians, defending themselves from Laconia against the Spartiates, prevailed, while the Lacedaemonians, having their own country as enemy territory, attacked the enemy from the sea; and it came about that those who prevailed on land held command of the sea, while those foremost at sea shut off the enemy from the land.

The Athenians, then, being honoured by Alexander above all the other Greeks, kept quiet; but most of the Peloponnesians and certain others, uniting in purpose, enrolled for the war, and, levying according to the strength of their cities the best of the young men, mustered soldiers not fewer than twenty thousand foot and about two thousand horse.
The Lacedaemonians, holding the leadership, set out with their whole people to the contest for everything, Agis the king having the command of all.

These things, then, were done in this year. When Phaion was archon at Athens, at Rome Lucius Furius Mediolanus and Marcus Manilius Vason succeeded to the consular office. In their time a great and unexpected calamity befell the Lacedaemonians; for, great earthquakes occurring in Sparta, it came about that the houses fell from their foundations and more than twenty thousand of the Lacedaemonians were destroyed.
As the siege dragged on, and the Athenians prevailed with their ships and prevented the bringing of grain into the land, those cut off on the island were in danger of being destroyed by famine.

To Sicily there put in Hermocrates the Syracusan. This man, having been general in the war against the Athenians and having become very useful to his native land, had the greatest power among the Syracusans; but afterward, having been sent as admiral with thirty-five triremes to ally with the Lacedaemonians, he was overthrown in faction by his political opponents, and became a condemned exile, and handed over the fleet in the Peloponnese to those sent for the succession.

He seized also the suburb of Achradine, and plundered the temples of Demeter and Core; for which he quickly paid a fitting penalty for his impiety toward the divine. For his affairs quickly grew worse day by day, and as Dionysius took courage to engage in skirmishes, it came to pass that the Syracusans had the advantage. 63.2. There arose also by night in the camp unaccountable confusions, and they ran together with their arms, as though the enemy were attacking the palisade. There came on also a disease, which became the cause of all evils to them; about which we shall speak a little later, that we may not anticipate in our narrative the proper times. 63.3. Himilcon, then, having thrown a wall about the camp, demolished almost all the tombs nearby, among which were those of Gelon and his wife Demarete, costly in their construction. He built also three forts along the sea, one on Plemmyrium, one in the middle of the harbour, and one by the temple of Zeus; into these he brought down the wine and the grain and the rest of the provisions, thinking the siege would be longer. 63.4. He sent off also the merchant-ships to Sardinia and Libya, that they might convey grain and the other supplies. Polyxenus the brother-in-law of Dionysius came from the Peloponnese and from Italy bringing thirty warships from the allies and as admiral Pharacidas the Lacedaemonian. 64.1. After this Dionysius and Leptines with the warships sailed out, wishing to convoy a supply of food; but the Syracusans, being by themselves and chancing to see a grain-ship bearing in, sailed out against it with five ships, and mastering it brought it into the city. 64.2. When the Carthaginians put out against them with forty ships, the Syracusans manned all their ships, and fighting at sea both mastered the flagship and destroyed twenty-four of the others; and pursuing those that fled as far as the enemy's naval station, they challenged the Carthaginians to a sea-battle. 64.3. They, then, being thrown into confusion by the surprise, kept quiet, while the Syracusans, taking in tow the captured ships, brought them into the city. Elated by their advantage, and reflecting that Dionysius had often been defeated, while they themselves without him had conquered the Carthaginians, they were filled with high spirit. 64.4. Gathering together they talked among themselves, that they looked on while they were slaves to Dionysius, and that too while they had an opportunity for his overthrow; for in the time before they had been disarmed, but now, because of the war, they were masters of their arms. 64.5. Nevertheless, such talk being current, Dionysius sailed in, and gathering an assembly praised the Syracusans and called upon them to be of good courage, promising that he would quickly bring the war to an end. And when he was now about to dissolve the assembly, Theodorus the Syracusan, well esteemed among the cavalry and seeming to be a man of action, ventured to use such words as these about freedom. 65.1. Even if Dionysius has told some falsehoods, yet what was said by him at the last was true, that he would quickly bring the war to an end. This he might be able to do, not by leading us himself—for he has often been defeated—but by giving back to the citizens their ancestral freedom. 65.2. For now no one of us willingly endures the dangers, when victory is no less than defeat; for if defeated we must do what the Carthaginians command, and if victorious we have in Dionysius a master more grievous than they. For the Carthaginians, even if they should master us in war, taking a fixed tribute would not hinder us from governing the city by our ancestral laws; but this man, having plundered the temples, and having taken away the wealth of private persons together with the lives of their owners, pays the servants as wages for the enslavement of their masters; and the terrible things that happen in the captures of cities, these he does in time of peace, and yet promises to end the war against the Carthaginians. 65.3. But for us, men, no less than the Phoenician war, must we end the tyrant within the wall. For the citadel, guarded by the arms of slaves, has been built up as a fortress against the city, and the multitude of mercenaries has been gathered for the enslavement of the Syracusans. And he rules the city, not dispensing justice on equal terms, but as a monarch deciding to do everything by greed. And now the enemy hold a small part of the country, but Dionysius, having made it all desolate, has bestowed it upon those who help to increase his tyranny. 65.4. How long, then, shall we endure to suffer these things, for which the good, that they may not make trial of them, submit to die? And, contending against the Carthaginians, we endure the utmost dangers stout-heartedly, but against a bitter tyrant we do not dare any longer, even in word, to keep free speech on behalf of freedom and of our fatherland; and against so many myriads of the enemy we set ourselves, but at a monarch who has not even the valour of a noble slave we shudder. 66.1. For surely no one would think it right to compare Dionysius with the ancient Gelon. For that man, with his own valour, together with the Syracusans and the other Sicilians, freed all Sicily; but this man, having received the cities in freedom, has made the enemy masters of all the rest, while he himself has enslaved his fatherland. 66.2. And that man, having fought far in advance of Sicily, did not let the allies in the cities even see the enemy; but this man, having fled from Motye through the whole island, has shut himself up within the walls, blustering against the citizens, but not enduring even to look the enemy in the face. 66.3. Therefore that man, both for his valour and for the magnitude of his deeds, received the leadership not only of the Syracusans but also of the Sicilians, with their willing consent; but this man, having generalled for the destruction of the allies and the enslavement of the citizens, how should he not justly be hated by all? For he is not only unworthy of leadership, but also deserves to meet with ten thousand deaths. 66.4. Gela and Camarina were overthrown because of him, Messene has been utterly destroyed, twenty thousand of the allies have perished in the sea-battle, and in sum we have been shut up in a single city, all the Greek cities in Sicily having been destroyed. For, besides his other wrongs, he reduced Naxos and Catane to slavery, allied cities, favourably situated cities, he has utterly destroyed. 66.5. And against the Carthaginians, having joined two battles, in each he has been defeated; but among the citizens, having once been entrusted with a generalship, he immediately took away their freedom, slaying those who kept free speech on behalf of the laws, banishing those pre-eminent in their possessions, and giving the wives of the exiles to slaves and to mongrel men, and making barbarians and foreigners masters of the citizens' arms. And these things he did, O Zeus and all the gods, a servant of magistrates' offices, a man given up for lost. 67.1. And where is the love of freedom of the Syracusans? Where the deeds of their forefathers? I pass over the three hundred thousand Carthaginians utterly destroyed at Himera, I leave aside the overthrow of the tyrants after Gelon; but yesterday and the day before, when the Athenians marched against Syracuse with so great forces, our fathers did not leave even the man to report the disaster. 67.2. But we, having such great examples of our fathers' valour, obey the commands of Dionysius, and this too when we are masters of our arms? Some providence of the gods, with our allies, has brought us together in arms for the recovery of freedom, and it is in our power today, having become good men and being of one mind, to be rid of grievous necessity. 67.3. For in the time before, being disarmed and destitute of allies, and held down by the multitude of the mercenaries, we yielded, as it were, to the necessity of the occasion; but now, being masters of our arms and having the allies at once as helpers and as spectators of our valour, let us not give way, but make it manifest that it was because of the occasion, not from cowardice, that we endured to be slaves. 67.4. Are we not ashamed to have as leader of the wars one who has plundered the temples in the city, and to make him champion of such great matters, to whom no one in his right mind would entrust the management of a private life? And while others, in their wars, most of all observe the duties toward the gods because of the magnitude of the dangers, do we hope that the man notorious for impiety will bring the war to an end?

The Lacedaemonians, having lost many of their young men in the calamity at Leuctra, and having lost not a few in the other defeats, and in sum being shut up by fortune into few citizen-soldiers, and besides this their allies, some having revolted, some for like causes being short of men, fell into great helplessness. Therefore they were compelled to flee for refuge to the aid of the Athenians, upon whom in former times they had set thirty tyrants, whom they had prevented from rebuilding the walls of their city, and whom they had attempted, by utterly destroying the city, to make Attica a sheep-pasture. 63.2. But indeed nothing is stronger than necessity and fortune, by which the Lacedaemonians were forced to beg of their bitterest enemies. Nevertheless they were not deceived of their hopes. For the people of the Athenians, being magnanimous and humane, were not struck with dismay at the strength of the Thebans, but voted to help the Lacedaemonians, who were in danger of being enslaved, in full force. And at once, appointing Iphicrates general, they sent out the young men on the same day, being twelve thousand. Iphicrates, then, having his soldiers eager, advanced with the force in haste. 63.3. The Lacedaemonians, the enemy encamping on the borders of Laconia, themselves also in full force making their going out from Sparta, advanced against their opponents, humbled in the forces of their soldiers, but confident in the virtues of their souls. 63.4. The men of Epaminondas, seeing the country of the Lacedaemonians hard to invade, did not think it of advantage to make the invasion in a single such great force, but dividing themselves into four parts decided to make the onset at several places. 64.1. The first part, that of the Boeotians, made its march in the middle against the city called Sellasia, and made those dwelling there revolt from the Lacedaemonians. 64.2. The Argives, invading by the borders of the Tegeatid country, joined battle with those guarding the passes, and both slew the leader of the garrison, Alexander the Spartan, and slew of the others about two hundred, among whom were also the exiles of the Boeotians. 64.3. The third part, composed of the Arcadians and having the most soldiers, invaded the country called the Sciritis, which Ischolas, a man distinguished in valour and understanding, was guarding with many soldiers. This man, of the most notable soldiers, accomplished a heroic deed worthy of memory. 64.4. For seeing that because of the multitude of the enemy all who joined battle would be slain, he judged it unworthy of Sparta to leave the post in the passes, but that to save the soldiers would be useful to the fatherland; therefore, unexpectedly he provided for both, and zealously imitated the valour of King Leonidas at Thermopylae of old. 64.5. For having picked out the young men, these he sent to Sparta, to be useful to her who was in danger about the whole; while he himself, with the elders, guarding the post and slaying many of the enemy, surrounded by the Arcadians, was slain with all his men. 64.6. The Eleians, having the fourth part, and going through other regions that were open, came to Hellasia; for to this place all had been ordered to come. The whole force being gathered at Hellasia, they advanced against Sparta itself, ravaging at the same time and burning the country. 65.1. The Lacedaemonians, having kept Laconia unravaged for five hundred years, then seeing it laid waste by the enemy, did not endure, but, rushing forward in their wrath, leaped out of the city; being prevented by the elders from advancing too far from their fatherland, lest someone attack, they were persuaded to keep quiet and to provide safety for the city. 65.2. The men of Epaminondas coming down through Taygetus to the Eurotas, and crossing the river, which was violent in its stream in the winter season, the Lacedaemonians, seeing the force of their opponents thrown into confusion because of the difficulty of the crossing, took a fit opportunity for an attack, and leaving the women and children, and besides the aged, in the city to guard Sparta, they themselves, having arrayed the young men in full force, poured out against the enemy, and falling suddenly upon those crossing, made much slaughter. 65.3. The Boeotians and Arcadians defending and surrounding their opponents by their multitude, the Spartans, having slain many, returned to the city, having manifestly displayed their own bravery. 65.4. After this, the men of Epaminondas attacking the city with the whole force strikingly, the Spartans, having as helper the strength of the places, slew many of those who rashly forced their way; and at last the besiegers, bringing in every zeal, at first hoped to master Sparta by force; but when of those who forced their way some died and some were wounded, the men of Epaminondas recalled the soldiers by the trumpet, and themselves, coming up to the city, challenged the Spartans to battle, or ordered them to agree that they were inferior to the enemy. 65.5. The Spartans answering that, taking a fit opportunity, they would fight it out for the whole, they departed from the city. Having ravaged all Laconia and gathered a countless multitude of booty, they withdrew to Arcadia. 65.6. After this the Athenians, being late for the occasions, returned to Attica, having done nothing worthy of memory; but to the Lacedaemonians there came from the allies four thousand soldiers to help. Besides these, adding the Helots lately freed, a thousand, and of the Boeotian exiles two hundred, and besides sending for not a few from the nearby cities, they prepared a force a match for the enemy. Immediately all the ships made their attack, and at the captures of the forts, the army having raised the war-cry, the barbarians were thrown into utter dread. arg.0. The contents of the thirteenth of the books of Diodorus. The expedition of the Athenians against the Syracusans with great land and naval forces. The voyage of the Athenians to Sicily. The recall of Alcibiades the general and his flight to Lacedaemon. How the Athenians, sailing across into the great harbor of the Syracusans, seized the places about the Olympieium. How the Athenians, having seized Epipolae and conquered in battle, besieged Syracuse from both sides. How, when the Lacedaemonians and Corinthians sent aid, the Syracusans took courage. A battle of the Syracusans and Athenians, and a great victory of the Athenians. A battle of the same, and a victory of the Syracusans. How the Syracusans, having gained control of Epipolae, compelled the Athenians to come into a single camp, the one by the Olympieium. How the Syracusans, having prepared a naval force, resolved to fight at sea. How the Athenians, Lamachus the general having died and Alcibiades having been recalled, sent in their place as generals Eurymedon and Demosthenes with a force and money. The breaking of the treaties by the Lacedaemonians and the war against the Athenians called the Peloponnesian. A sea-battle of the Syracusans and Athenians and a victory of the Athenians, and the capture of forts by the Syracusans and a victory on land. A sea-battle with all the ships in the great harbor and a victory of the Syracusans. The voyage from Athens of Demosthenes and Eurymedon with a notable force. A great battle about Epipolae and a victory of the Syracusans. The flight of the Athenians and the capture of the whole force. How the Syracusans, having come together in assembly, set forth a deliberation how they ought to deal with the captives. The speeches delivered on each side of the question. The things voted by the Syracusans concerning the captives. How, the Athenians having stumbled about Sicily, many of the allies revolted. How the people of the Athenians, having become despondent, gave up the democracy and entrusted the constitution to four hundred men. How the Lacedaemonians conquered the Athenians in the sea-battles. How the Syracusans honored with notable gifts those who had behaved bravely in the war. How Diocles, chosen as lawgiver, wrote the laws for the Syracusans. How the Syracusans sent a notable force to the Lacedaemonians. How the Athenians, having defeated the admiral of the Lacedaemonians in a sea-battle, took Cyzicus by siege. How, the Lacedaemonians having sent fifty ships from Euboea to the aid of the defeated, all were destroyed with their men about Athos by the storm. The return of Alcibiades and his generalship. The war of the Egestaeans and Selinuntians over the disputed land. How the Lacedaemonians, having dammed up the Euripus, made Euboea mainland. On the faction and slaughter that took place in Corcyra. A sea-battle of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians about Sigeium and a victory of the Athenians. How Alcibiades and Theramenes conquered the Lacedaemonians most brilliantly both by land and by sea. How the Carthaginians, having ferried great forces into Sicily, took Selinus and Himera by storm. How Alcibiades, having sailed into the Piraeus with much booty, met with great acceptance. How Agis the king, having undertaken to besiege Athens with a great force, was driven off. The flight of Alcibiades, and the founding of Therma in Sicily. A sea-battle of the Syracusans against the Carthaginians and a victory of the Syracusans. On the prosperity in Acragas and the constructions in it. How the Carthaginians, having campaigned into Sicily with three hundred thousand, besieged Acragas. How the Syracusans, having taken along the allies, came to the aid of the Acragantines with ten thousand soldiers. How, forty thousand Carthaginians having met them, the Syracusans conquered and cut down more than six thousand. How, the Carthaginians cutting off the provisions, the Acragantines, because of the lack of food, were compelled to abandon their native land. How Dionysius, chosen as general, became tyrant of the Syracusans. How the Athenians, having conquered in a most brilliant sea-battle at Arginusae, unjustly put their generals to death. We, being accustomed to add to the ends of good men their own praise, in no way think it fitting to pass over unmarked the death of so great a man. For Pausanias, being his pupil, and during the lecture asking how one might become most famous, the sophist answered: "If he should slay the one who has done the greatest deeds; for, by the memory of him, the one who made away with him would be included as well."

Seeing that his soldiers were worn down by the continuous campaigns and had toiled for nearly eight years in labours and dangers, he supposed it necessary to urge the multitude with fitting words toward the campaign against the Gandaridae.

The reason why they were doing this he had known even before, but now had learned more clearly; for Himilco had sent a herald to him, with the pretext of the captives, but to urge that—the multitude of his fellow-magistrates, having secured themselves, busied themselves with nothing of what was being done—he should at least not oppose, since he chose not to cooperate.
Referring the saying to his own anger, and, through his passion, making no postponement of the resolution, he set up the plot in the very contests then taking place, in some such manner as this.

For there had been much destruction of the soldiers, and no end of the wars was hoped for; and the horses, through the continuousness of the march, had their hooves worn away, while most of the arms were worn out, and the Greek clothing had given out, so that they were compelled to use barbarian fabrics, cutting up the wrappings of the Indians.

Therefore he no longer wished to be general, but was present to lay down his office; for it was not tolerable that, the others selling their native land, he alone should run risks with the citizens and at the same time seem to have shared in the treason.

Stationing horses at the gates, he came to the entrances of the theatre, having a Celtic dagger concealed. When Philip ordered the friends who attended him to go on ahead into the theatre, and the bodyguards were standing apart, seeing the king alone, he ran up, and dealing a thrust through the ribs, stretched out the king a corpse, and himself ran toward the gates and the horses prepared for the flight.

By chance, too, fierce storms burst forth for seventy days, and continuous thunder and lightning fell. Reckoning that these things opposed his own designs, he had one hope of his desire: if he should win his soldiers to great goodwill through benefaction.

The crowd being provoked at what was said, and the speech flowing through the whole force, then each man, in anxiety, withdrew home; but on the next day, an assembly having been gathered, in which he accused the magistrates of many things, he met with no moderate approval, and provoked the people against the generals.

Straightway some of the bodyguards rushed to the body of the king, while others poured out in pursuit of the murderer, among whom were Leonnatus and Perdiccas and Attalus. Pausanias, having got a lead of the pursuit, would have outstripped it by leaping onto his horse, had not his sandal caught about a certain vine and he fell. Wherefore Perdiccas and his men, overtaking him as he was rising from the ground, ran him through and slew him.

Therefore he allowed them to plunder the enemy's country, which was full of every kind of booty; and during the days when the force was occupied in foraging, gathering the wives of the soldiers and the children born of them, he arranged to give the women grain monthly, and assigned to the children allowances by company, according to the reckonings of their fathers.

Finally, some of those seated cried out to make him general plenipotentiary and not to wait until the enemy should come up to the walls; for the magnitude of the war needed such a general, through whom it was possible to be well off in affairs; the matters concerning the traitors they would deliberate in another assembly; for it was foreign to the present occasions; and previously too the three hundred thousand of the Carthaginians had been conquered at Himera, Gelon being general plenipotentiary.

When the soldiers returned, having found a great quantity of good things from the foraging, he gathered them all into an assembly. Having delivered a carefully prepared speech about the campaign against the Gandaridae, and the Macedonians by no means consenting, he desisted from the enterprise.

The many quickly inclining, as is their wont, to the worse, Dionysius was declared general plenipotentiary. And when, then, affairs followed according to his mind, he wrote a decree that the wages should be double; for, he said, this being done, all would be more eager for the contest, and concerning the money he urged them to be in no anxiety; for the means for it would be easy.

The Carthaginians, slowly recovering themselves from the disaster about Syracuse, resolved to hold fast to their affairs in Sicily. Deciding to fight it out, they crossed over with a few warships, but gathered a force from Libya and Sardinia, and besides from the barbarians in Italy. Having carefully armed all with their proper equipment, they crossed over into Sicily, being not fewer than eighty thousand, whom Mago led. 95.2. He, then, marching through the country of the Sicels, and causing most of the cities to revolt from Dionysius, encamped in the territory of the Agyrinaeans by the river Chrysas near the road leading to Morgantine; for, being unable to bring over the Agyrinaeans into alliance, he gave up his forward march, hearing that the enemy had set out from Syracuse. 95.3. Dionysius, learning that the Carthaginians were making their march through the interior, quickly collected as many as he could of the Syracusans and the mercenaries and set out, having in all not fewer than twenty thousand. 95.4. Coming near the enemy, he sent an embassy to Agyris the ruler of the Agyrinaeans. This man had the greatest power of the tyrants then in Sicily after Dionysius; for he was master of almost all the surrounding strongholds and ruled the city of the Agyrinaeans, which was much-peopled at those times; for it had citizens not fewer than twenty thousand. 95.5. There was also gathered in this great multitude in the city, in the citadel, a store of much money, which Agyris had amassed by murdering the wealthiest of the citizens. 95.6. But Dionysius, entering within the wall with a few, persuaded Agyris to ally himself genuinely, and promised to give him much of the bordering country, the war being brought to a successful issue. 95.7. Agyris, then, first eagerly gave to the whole force of Dionysius grain and the other things that were needed, and leading out his force in full strength campaigned with Dionysius and made war in common against the Carthaginians. 96.1. Mago, encamping in a hostile country, and ever becoming more in want of necessaries, was no moderately at a disadvantage; for the troops of Agyris, being experienced in the country, had the advantage in the ambushes and took away the provisions of the enemy. 96.2. When the Syracusans said that they should decide affairs by battle as quickly as possible, Dionysius opposed, saying that without dangers the barbarians would be destroyed by time and scarcity; at which the Syracusans, being enraged, abandoned Dionysius. 96.3. He at first, in caution, called the household-slaves to freedom, but after this, the Carthaginians sending an embassy about peace, he gave heed and made them sendable back to their masters, and with the Carthaginians made peace. 96.4. The terms were in other respects similar to the former, but that the Sicels should be ranged under Dionysius and that he should take over Tauromenium. After the treaty Mago sailed off, while Dionysius, taking over Tauromenium, cast out most of the Sicels there, and choosing the most suitable of his own mercenaries settled them there. 96.5. And the affairs in Sicily were in this state, while in Italy the Romans took by storm Faliscus, a city of the nation of the Falisci. 97.1. This year having passed, at Athens Nicoteles was archon, and at Rome three military tribunes administered the consular office, Marcus Furius, Gaius Aemilius. These having taken over the office, those of the Rhodians who favoured Sparta, rising up against the people, cast out of the city those who favoured the Athenians. 97.2. These running together in arms and attempting to hold fast to affairs, those allied with the Lacedaemonians prevailed, and slew many, and proclaimed the survivors banished. Immediately too they sent envoys to Lacedaemon for help, fearing lest some of the citizens make a revolution. 97.3. The Lacedaemonians sent them seven triremes and three men to take charge of affairs, Eudocimus and Philodocus and Diphilas. These, first conveyed to Samos, caused the city to revolt from the Athenians, then sailing to Rhodes had the management of affairs there. 97.4. The Lacedaemonians, their affairs proceeding for them, resolved to hold fast to the sea, and again, little by little, prevailed over the allies, having gathered a fleet. These, then, sailed to Samos and Cnidus and Rhodes, and from every side enrolling ships and the best marines, they fitted out lavishly twenty-seven triremes. 97.5. Agesilaus the king of the Lacedaemonians, hearing that the Argives were staying about Corinth, led out the Lacedaemonians in full force except for one division. Going over all Argolis, he plundered the possessions, and cutting down the trees of the country withdrew to Sparta.

In the archonship at Athens of Nicophemus, the consular office at Rome was held by Gaius Sulpicius and Gaius Licinius. In this year Alexander the tyrant of Pherae, sending piratical ships against the Cyclades islands, took some by siege and gained possession of many persons, and, disembarking mercenary soldiers at Peparethos, besieged the city. 95.2. The Athenians coming to the aid of the Peparethians, and leaving Leosthenes as general, he attacked the Athenians; these happened to be watching those of Alexander's soldiers staying at Panormus. The men of the ruler attacking unexpectedly, a paradoxical success came about for Alexander. For not only did he save those sent to Panormus from the greatest dangers, but he also took five Attic triremes and one Peparethian, and gained possession of six hundred persons. 95.3. The Athenians, provoked, condemned Leosthenes to death as a traitor and confiscated his property, and choosing Chares general and giving him a naval force, sent him out. He continued, on the one hand being on his guard against the enemy, and on the other wronging the allies. For sailing to Corcyra, an allied city, he stirred up great factions in it, from which it came to pass that there were many slaughters and plunderings, through which it happened that the people of the Athenians were slandered among the allies. Chares, then, committing other such lawless deeds, accomplished nothing good, but slanders for his fatherland. 95.4. Of the historians, Dionysodorus and Anaxis the Boeotians closed their works on Greek history at this year. We, having traversed the deeds before Philip the king, in accordance with our purpose at the beginning conclude this book here, and the following one, beginning from the accession of Philip to the kingdom, we shall go through all the deeds of this king down to his death, including also the other deeds that occurred in the known parts of the inhabited world.

arg.0. The following is contained in the sixteenth of Diodorus's historical books. How Philip the son of Amyntas succeeded to the kingdom of the Macedonians. How he defeated Argaeus, who was a rival claimant to the kingdom. How, having subdued the Illyrians and Paeonians, he won back his ancestral dominion. Concerning the unmanliness of the younger Dionysius and the flight of Dion. The founding of Tauromenium in Sicily. The events in Euboea and in the Social War. The siege of Amphipolis by Philip and its capture. How Philip enslaved the people of Pydna and developed the gold mines. How Dion, after liberating the Syracusans, made war upon Dionysius. How, after being driven from his native land, he recovered Syracuse again. The ending of the Social War. The combination of three kings against Philip. How Philomelus the Phocian, having seized Delphi and the oracle, kindled the Sacred War. Concerning the original discovery of the oracle. The defeat and death of Philomelus the Phocian. Onomarchus's assumption of the command and his preparations for war. How the Boeotians, coming to the aid of Artabazus, defeated the King's satraps. How the Athenians, having gained control of the Chersonese, allotted it to colonists. How Philip, after taking Methone, razed it. How Philip, having defeated the Phocians, drove them out of Thessaly. How Onomarchus the Phocian, having defeated Philip in two battles, brought him into the utmost peril. How Onomarchus, having defeated the Boeotians, took Coroneia. How Onomarchus, drawing up his forces in Thessaly against Philip and the Thessalians, was defeated. How he himself was hanged, while the others were cast into the sea as temple-robbers. How Phayllus, succeeding to the command, cut up many of the silver and gold offerings. How, by raising the rates of pay, he gathered a multitude of mercenaries. How he restored the fallen fortunes of the Phocians. How, by corrupting with money the cities and their leading men, he won over many allies. How the tyrants of Pherae, surrendering Pherae to Philip, became allies of the Phocians. The battle of the Phocians against the Boeotians near Orchomenus and the defeat of the Phocians. Other battles between the same peoples by the Cephisus and at Coroneia, and the victory of the Boeotians. How Phayllus, marching into Locris, subdued many cities. How Phayllus, falling into a wasting disease, ended his life in suffering. How Phalaecus, succeeding to the command and conducting the war ignobly, was driven out. How those in the Peloponnese fell into civil strife. How Artaxerxes, surnamed Ochus, recovered Egypt and Phoenicia and Cyprus. How Philip, after winning over the Chalcidian cities, razed the most notable city. The inquiry into the sacred treasures that had been expended and the punishment of those who had embezzled them. How those Phocians who took refuge in the temple of Apollo, being five hundred in number, all perished, paradoxically, by fire. How the Phocian War was brought to an end. How all those who had shared in the sacrilege with the Phocians were punished by some divine agency. Timoleon's voyage to Sicily and his exploits down to his death. The siege of Perinthus and Byzantium by Philip. Philip's pitched battle against the Athenians at Chaeronea and the defeat of the Athenians. How the Greeks chose Philip general with full powers. How Philip, when about to cross into Asia, was assassinated.

Philip, then, having become the greatest of the kings in Europe in his time, and through the magnitude of his rule having counted himself enthroned together with the twelve gods, met with such an end of his life, having ruled twenty-four years.

Having resolved to set the limits of his campaign at this point, he first built altars of the twelve gods fifty cubits high; then, marking out a camp three times the size of the former, he dug a trench fifty feet wide and forty deep, and, heaping the excavated earth within the trench, built a considerable wall.

The assembly having been dissolved, not a few of the Syracusans found fault with what had been done, as though they themselves had not ratified these things; for, coming in their reckonings to themselves, they considered the despotism that would come to be. They, then, wishing to make their freedom firm, had without their noticing established a master of their native land;

This king is held to have taken over the slenderest resources for the monarchy, but to have acquired the greatest of the monarchies among the Greeks, and to have increased his leadership not so much through valour in arms as through intercourse and graciousness in words.

He ordered each of the foot to build lodgings having two beds five cubits long, and the cavalry, besides these, two mangers double the usual size; and in keeping with this he ordered the other things that were to be left behind to be increased in size. This he intended to do, both wishing to make a heroic camp, and to leave to the inhabitants tokens of great men, displaying the prodigious strength of their bodies.

and Dionysius, wishing to anticipate the repentance of the crowds, sought how he might ask for guards for his person; for, this being conceded, he would easily master the tyranny. At once, then, he ordered all of military age up to forty years, taking provisions for thirty days, to come under arms to Leontini. This city was then a fort of the Syracusans, full of exiles and foreigners. For he hoped to have these as fellow-fighters, desiring change, and that the most of the Syracusans would not even come to Leontini.
And they say that Philip himself prided himself more on his shrewdness in generalship and on his successes through intercourse than on his courage in battles;

Having done with these things, he marched with his whole force by the same roads and came back to the river Acesines; and, finding the boats built, and having refitted these, he built others in addition.

Nevertheless, by night encamping in the country and pretending to be plotted against, he made an outcry and tumult through his own servants; having done this, he fled together into the acropolis, and passed the night, burning fires and summoning the most notable of the soldiers.
for of the successes in the struggles all who campaigned shared, but of the successes that came through intercourse he alone received the credit.

At this time there came from Greece allies and mercenaries, led by the generals: more than thirty thousand foot and not much short of six thousand horse; and there were also brought splendid suits of armour for twenty-five thousand foot, and a hundred talents of medicinal drugs. These, then, he distributed to the soldiers.

At daybreak, the multitude having gathered to Leontini, having spoken much plausibly to the purpose of his design, he persuaded the crowds to give him as guards six hundred of the soldiers, whichever he should choose. Dionysius is said to have done this imitating Pisistratus the Athenian;
But we, since we have arrived at the death of Philip, shall here close this book, according to the purpose set forth at the beginning, and shall make the next the starting-point of the following.

arg.0. The following is contained in the first of the two divisions of the seventeenth of Diodorus's books. How Alexander, having succeeded to the kingdom, ordered the affairs of his realm. How he recovered the nations that were in revolt. How, having razed Thebes and struck fear into the Greeks, he was chosen general with full powers of Greece. How, having crossed into Asia, he defeated the satraps at the river Granicus in Phrygia. How he reduced Miletus and Halicarnassus by siege. The battle of Darius against Alexander at Issus in Cilicia, and Alexander's victory. The siege of Tyre, the taking over of Egypt, and the king's journey to Ammon. The pitched battle at Arbela between Alexander and Darius, and Alexander's victory. The battle of Antipater against the Lacedaemonians, and Antipater's victory. The second division contains the following. The capture of Arbela by Alexander, and the seizure of much treasure. The recovery of the army at Babylon, and the gifts given to those who had distinguished themselves for valour. The arrival of the mercenaries and allies who had been sent for. The disposition and equipping of the army. How Alexander took over Susa and the treasures in it. How he gained control of the passes and mastered what are called the Susian Gates. How he showed kindness to the mutilated Greeks, and took over and plundered Persepolis. How in his revelry he set fire to the palace. The death of Darius at the hands of Bessus. Alexander's campaign into Hyrcania, and an account of the marvels that grow there. How Alexander, campaigning against the Mardians, subdued that nation. How Thalestris, the queen of the Amazons, had intercourse with Alexander. How the king, thinking himself invincible, came to emulate the luxury of the Persians. The campaign of Alexander against the Areians who had revolted, and the capture of the Rock. The plot against the king and the punishment of those who attacked him, the most distinguished of whom were Parmenion and Philotas. Alexander's campaign against the Paropanisadae, and what was done in it. The single combat that took place among the Areians, and the taking over of that nation. The death of Bessus, who had killed Darius. How Alexander, marching through the waterless country, lost many of his soldiers. How Alexander put to death the Branchidae, who in ancient times had been resettled by the Persians to the farthest parts of the kingdom, as traitors to the Greeks. How the king campaigned against the Sogdians and the Scythians. How the leading men of the Sogdians, as they were being led off to their death, were unexpectedly saved. How Alexander reduced the Sogdians who had revolted, and slaughtered more than a hundred and twenty thousand of them. How he punished the Bactrians, subdued the Sogdians a second time, and founded cities well placed for the chastisement of those who revolted. The third revolt of the Sogdians, and the capture of those who had taken refuge on the Rock. Concerning the hunt at Basista and the multitude of beasts in it. Concerning the offence against Dionysus and the slaying of Cleitus over the wine. Concerning the death of Callisthenes. The king's campaign against the people called the Nautacae, and the destruction of the army by heavy snow. How Alexander, falling in love with Roxane the daughter of Oxyartes, married her, and persuaded many of his friends to marry the daughters of the distinguished barbarians. The preparation for the campaign against the Indians. The invasion of India, and the utter destruction of the first nation as a terror to the rest. How he showed kindness to the city called Nysa because of its kinship with Dionysus. How, having stormed the strong city of Massaca, he cut down all the mercenaries, who had fought brilliantly. How he reduced by siege the Rock called Aornus, which had always remained impregnable. How he won over Taxiles the king of the Indians, and, having defeated Porus in a great battle and taken him captive, restored the kingdom to him because of his valour. An account of the marvellous serpents and the fruits that grow in that country. How he won over some of the neighbouring nations and subdued others by war. How he subdued the country governed by Sopeithes. Concerning the good order of the cities in that country. Concerning the excellence of the dogs given to Alexander. Concerning the narrative of the king of the Indians. How, when Alexander wished to cross the river Ganges and march against the people called the Gandaridae, the Macedonians refused to obey. How the king, setting limits to his campaign, traversed the rest of India. How he sailed down the river Indus to the Ocean toward the south, and was struck by an arrow and endangered. Concerning the single combat that took place upon a challenge. Concerning the Indians who were subdued on both sides of the river as far as the Ocean. Concerning the marvels and customs among the inhabitants, and those who lead a bestial life. How those who had sailed the Ocean joined Alexander, who had encamped by the sea, and reported what had happened on the voyage. How, having put out to sea again, they sailed along much of the coastal country. How, having picked thirty thousand young Persians and trained them in the works of war, he made of them a counterpart to the Macedonian phalanx. How Harpalus, slandered for his luxury and the excess of his expenditures, fled from Babylon and became a suppliant of the Athenian people. How, escaping from Attica, he was put to death; and of his treasures he had deposited seven hundred talents with the Athenians, but left four thousand talents and eight thousand mercenaries at Taenarum in Laconia. How Alexander discharged the debts of the aged Macedonians, spending ten thousand talents, and released them to their homelands. How, when the Macedonians mutinied, he punished those responsible. How Peucestes brought to Alexander ten thousand archers and slingers picked from among the Persians. How the king formed his units by mixing Persians with the Macedonians. How he supplied the ten thousand sons born of the soldiers with maintenance and the wages of education, for all of them. How Leosthenes began to stir up the war against the Macedonians. How Alexander campaigned against the Cossaeans. How, as the king was journeying to Babylon, the Chaldaeans foretold to Alexander that he would die if he entered Babylon. How the king at first was alarmed and passed Babylon by, but afterward, persuaded by the Greek philosophers, came down to the city. Concerning the multitude of embassies that arrived. Concerning the burial of Hephaestion and the multitude of riches spent upon it. Concerning the signs that appeared to Alexander, and his death.

The naval preparation being completed, and two hundred open vessels and eight hundred service-boats having been made ready, he named the cities founded along the river: the one, because he had conquered in the war, Nicaea, and the other, after the horse that died in the battle against Porus, Bucephala.

for they say that he too, having wounded himself, came forward into the assembly as having been plotted against, and for this reason got a guard from the citizens, by which, using it, he won the tyranny. And then Dionysius, by a like device, having deceived the multitude, set in motion the things of the tyranny.

For at once, having picked out those needy of money but bold in soul, more than a thousand, he armed them with costly arms and elated them with the greatest promises, and, summoning the mercenaries and using kind words, made them his own. He changed also the commands, handing over the offices to the most trustworthy, and released Dexippus the Lacedaemonian to Greece; for he was suspicious of this man, lest, getting an opportunity, he should recover freedom for the Syracusans.

He himself, with his friends, embarking on the ships, made the voyage through the river toward the Ocean in the south. The greater part of the force marched along the river, Craterus and Hephaestion leading. When they came to the junction of the Acesines and the Hydaspes, having disembarked the soldiers, he advanced against the people called the Sibi.

He summoned also the mercenaries in Gela, and gathered from every side the exiles and impious men, hoping through these most firmly to keep the tyranny. Nevertheless, having come to Syracuse, he quartered in the dockyard, openly declaring himself tyrant. The Syracusans, bearing it heavily, were compelled to keep quiet; for they could no longer accomplish anything, since the city was full of foreign arms, and they feared the Carthaginians, who had so great forces.

These, they say, are descendants of those who campaigned with Heracles against the rock Aornus and, having failed in the siege, were settled in this place by Heracles. Alexander encamping near their most famous city, the foremost in reputation among the citizens came forth. Meeting the king and renewing their kinship, they said that they would do everything with eagerness, as being kinsmen, and brought magnificent gifts.

Dionysius, then, immediately married the daughter of Hermocrates, who had defeated the Athenians, and gave his sister to Polyxenus, the brother of the wife of Hermocrates; this he did, wishing to take into kinship a distinguished house, with a view to making the tyranny firm. After this, having gathered an assembly, he killed the most powerful of those who had opposed him, Daphnaeus and Demarchus.

Alexander, accepting their goodwill and declaring the cities free, advanced toward the bordering nations. Finding the people called the Agalasseis having gathered forty thousand foot and three thousand horse, he joined battle with them and conquered, cut down most, and, having reduced by siege the rest who had fled together into the neighbouring cities, sold them into slavery.

Dionysius, then, from a scribe and a chance private man, became tyrant of the greatest of the Greek cities; and he preserved his dominion until his death, having been tyrant thirty-eight years. His particular deeds and the increase of his rule we shall go through in their proper times; for this man seems to have won for himself the greatest of recorded tyrannies, and the most long-lasting.

Of the other inhabitants who had gathered together, twenty thousand having fled into a great city, he took it by storm; and, the Indians having blocked the narrow streets and fighting stoutly from the houses, in forcing his way he lost not a few of the Macedonians.

The Carthaginians, after the capture of the city, transferred the votive offerings and statues and the other most costly things to Carthage, and, having burned the temples and plundered the city, wintered there. For the spring season they prepared engines and missiles of all kinds, intending to besiege first the city of the Geloans.

In his anger setting fire to the city, he burned up most of them; but of the remaining ones, about three thousand who had fled together into the citadel and begged him with suppliant branches, he released.

While these things were being done, the Athenians, continually falling into reverses, made citizens of the metics and of the other foreigners those who wished to fight together with them; and quickly, a great multitude having been enrolled as citizens, the generals enrolled the suitable for the expedition. They prepared sixty ships, and, having fitted these out costlily, sailed out to Samos, where they found the other generals having gathered from the other islands eighty triremes.

He himself, again embarking on the ships with his friends, made the voyage through the river to the junction of the rivers mentioned and the Indus. Great streams dashing together into one place, many fearful whirlpools arose, and, whirling the boats round, destroyed them. The violence of the stream being sharp and fierce, and the skill of the steersmen being overpowered, two warships sank, and not a few of the other vessels were cast ashore.
Having asked also the Samians to man ten triremes in addition, they put out with all the ships, being a hundred and fifty, and put in at the Arginusae islands, eager to raise the siege of Mitylene.

The flagship falling into a great cataract, the king came into the utmost danger. Therefore, death being before his eyes, Alexander, casting off his clothing, with his body bare clung to such help as was possible, and his friends swam beside him, eager to receive the king as the ship was overturned.

Callicratidas the admiral of the Lacedaemonians, learning of the approach of the ships, left Eteonicus with the land force at the siege, while he himself, having manned a hundred and forty ships, in haste put out toward the other side of the Arginusae; these islands were then inhabited and had a small Aeolic town, lying between Mitylene and Cyme, at a very short distance from the mainland and from the cape Canis.

There being much confusion about the ship, and the men setting themselves against the violence of the stream, but the river overpowering all human device and strength, Alexander with difficulty, along with the ships, was cast ashore. Having been unexpectedly saved, he sacrificed to the gods as having escaped the greatest dangers and as having contended against a river like Achilles.

The Athenians immediately learned of the approach of the enemy, lying at anchor not far off, but, because of the magnitude of the winds, gave up fighting at sea, and for the next day prepared the things for the sea-battle, the Lacedaemonians doing the same, although the seers forbade both.

For the head of the victim, lying on the shore of the Lacedaemonians, had become invisible, the wave washing over it; therefore the seer foretold that the admiral would die fighting at sea; at which the saying, they say Callicratidas said that, dying in the battle, he would make Sparta no less reputable.

Of the Athenians the general Thrasyllus, who was in command that day, saw in the night such a vision: it seemed that at Athens, the theater being full, he himself and six of the other generals were acting the tragedy of Euripides, the Phoenician Women, while their opponents acted the Suppliant Women, and it seemed that a Cadmean victory befell them, and that all died imitating the affairs of those who campaigned against Thebes.

The seer, hearing this, made plain that seven of the generals would be killed. The sacrifices bringing victory, the generals forbade announcing to the others concerning their own destruction, but concerning the victory in the sacrifices they announced throughout the whole force.

Callicratidas the admiral, having gathered the multitudes and encouraged them with suitable words, finally said: "For the danger on behalf of my native land I am myself so eager that, though the seer says that to you victory is foreshown by the victims, but to me death, nevertheless I am ready to die. Knowing, then, that after the death of leaders armies fall into tumult, I now declare as admiral, if I suffer anything, my successor Clearchus, a man who has given proof of his deeds in war."

In Cyprus Evagoras the Salaminian, who was most nobly born—for he was a descendant of the founders of the city—having gone into exile in the time before because of certain factions, and afterward returning with a few, cast out Abdemon the Tyrian, who was ruling the city and was a friend of the King of the Persians, while he himself, holding the city, at first reigned over Salamis, the greatest and most powerful of the cities in Cyprus; quickly being well supplied with much money and preparing a force, he attempted to make the whole island his own. 98.2. These having taken over the office, the Lacedaemonians, distressed by the war both against the Greeks and against the Persians, sent out Antalcidas the admiral to Artaxerxes about peace. 110.3. He having spoken acceptably about the matters for which he had been sent, the King said that he would make the peace on these terms: that the Greek cities in Asia be ranged under the King, and all the other Greeks be independent; and that against those who disobeyed and did not accept the treaty he would make war through those who consented. 110.4. The Lacedaemonians, then, being content with these terms, kept quiet, but the Athenians and Thebans and certain others of the Greeks took it ill that the cities in Asia were abandoned; but not being a match by themselves, of necessity they consented and accepted the peace. 110.5. And the King, the difference with the Greeks being settled, prepared his forces for the Cyprian war; for Evagoras had acquired almost the whole of Cyprus and had gathered strong forces, because Artaxerxes was distracted by the war against the Greeks. 111.1. Dionysius having besieged Rhegium nearly eleven months and shut off the reinforcements from every quarter, those in the city came into a terrible scarcity of necessaries; for they say that among the Rhegians at that time a medimnus of grain came to five minas. 111.2. Being worn down by the want of food, at first they ate up the horses and the other baggage-animals, and after this, boiling the hides they ate them, but at the last, going out of the city, they ate the grass by the walls like a kind of cattle; so did the necessity of nature force human diet to take refuge in the food of irrational animals. 111.3. Dionysius, learning what was happening, so far from pitying those compelled to suffer beyond what is human, on the contrary, bringing in yokes, took up the grass of the place, so that all the herbage was made to disappear. 111.4. Therefore, overcome by the excess of their ills, the Rhegians surrendered the city to the tyrant, giving up to him every authority over themselves. Dionysius found in the city heaps of corpses, who had died for want of food; and finding the living too in the condition of corpses and with their bodies enfeebled, he gathered captives more than six thousand. The multitude, then, he sent off to Syracuse, ordering those who gave a mina of silver to be ransomed, and those who could not provide it he sold as booty. 112.1. Phyton, the general of the Rhegians, having seized him, he sank his son in the sea, but the man himself at first he bound to the highest engines, taking, as it were, a kind of tragic vengeance, and sent one of his servants to say to him that yesterday Dionysius had sunk his son in the sea; to whom Phyton said that he had become more fortunate than his father by one day. 112.2. After this Dionysius led him round the city, scourging him and maltreating him in every way, while a herald followed, saying that Dionysius was taking extraordinary vengeance upon the man, because he had persuaded the city to choose war. 112.3. But Phyton, who had been a good general in the siege and was praised in the rest of his life, endured not ignobly the vengeance at his death, but, keeping his soul undismayed and crying out that he was meeting this vengeance because he had not been willing to betray the city to Dionysius, and that the divinity would speedily set the like upon Dionysius himself; so that the man's virtue was pitied even among the soldiers of Dionysius, and some were already raising an uproar. 112.4. Dionysius, fearing lest some of the soldiers should dare to snatch away Phyton, ceasing from the vengeance, sank the unfortunate man together with his kindred. 112.5. This man, then, unworthily of his virtue, met with lawless vengeances, and had even then many of the Greeks who grieved at his misfortune, and afterward poets who lamented the piteous nature of his reversal.

When Anticles was archon at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Lucius Cornelius and Quintus Popillius. In their time Alexander filled up the number of those discharged from among the Persians, and stationed a thousand of them as shield-bearers about the court, and supposed them in general no less to be trusted than the Macedonians.

for these, being of two tongues, in the one language are assimilated to the inhabitants, but in the other preserve most of the Greek words and keep up some of their pursuits. in which Hephaestion, indulging in unseasonable drinking and falling into illness, departed life. The king, taking the event hard, handed over the body of the dead man to Perdiccas to convey to Babylon, wishing to make his burial most splendid.

After this, having gathered a council of his friends, he deliberated about the war. While this was going on, in Greece disturbances arose and movements of revolution, from which the war called the Lamian War took its beginning, from some such cause as this. The king having ordered all the satraps to disband the mercenaries, and they having carried out the order, many mercenaries released from service ran about throughout all Asia, wandering and providing their necessary food from plunder. After this they crossed from all quarters to Taenarum in Laconia.

To these it had been ordered to burn fires throughout the whole night and to make noise, in order to give the Carthaginians the notion that he was remaining in the city. Likewise the surviving Persian satraps and the other commanders, gathering money and soldiers, sailed to Taenarum and gathered a common force.

Dionysius, having come to Camarina, compelled those there too, with their children and wives, to depart to Syracuse. The fear giving no respite, some packed up silver and gold and the things easily carried, others, taking their parents and infant children, fled, making no account of their property; some, being aged or weighed down by disease, for lack of kinsmen or friends were left behind, the Carthaginians being expected at any moment;

At last they chose as general with full powers Leosthenes the Athenian, a man distinguished for brilliance of spirit and most opposed to the affairs of Alexander. He, having conferred with the council in secret, received fifty talents for the pay and a sufficient quantity of arms for the pressing needs; and he sent envoys to the Aetolians, who were ill-disposed toward the king, about an alliance, and made all his preparations for the war.

for the calamity about Selinus and Himera, and besides Acragas, struck men, all as it were taking under their eyes the dreadful nature of the Carthaginians. Leosthenes, then, foreseeing the magnitude of the war, was engaged in these things. Alexander, the Cossaeans being disobedient, campaigned against them with a light-equipped force. This nation, distinguished for its valour, inhabits the hill country of Media, and, trusting in the difficulty of the ground and in its valour in war, had never received a foreign master, but had remained unsubdued even under the Persian kingdom; and then, being full of spirit, it was not dismayed at the valour of the Macedonians.

Nevertheless, two cities being driven out, the country was full of women and children and the other crowds; observing which, the soldiers were angry with Dionysius, but pitied the fortunes of the unfortunate;

The king, having occupied the passes beforehand and ravaged most of Cossaea, and having the advantage in all the engagements, killed many of the barbarians and took alive many times more. The Cossaeans, being everywhere defeated and taking it hard because of the multitude of those captured, were compelled to exchange slavery for the safety of their prisoners.
