When he was three hundred stadia from Babylon, the men called the Chaldaeans, who had won the greatest reputation in astrology and were accustomed, by a certain age-long observation, to foretell what was to come, chose out from among themselves the oldest and most experienced, and, having learned through the divination of the stars that the king's death would take place in Babylon, ordered them to disclose the danger to the king and to urge him by no means to make his entrance into the city;

The Italiotes, then, abandoning him, made their march homeward through the interior, while the cavalry of the Syracusans at first watched, to see if they could kill the tyrant on the road; but when they saw the mercenaries not abandoning him, with one accord they rode off to Syracuse.

Finding those in the dockyards ignorant of the affairs about Gela, they entered with none preventing, and plundered the house of Dionysius, full of silver and gold and all the other costliness, and, having seized his wife, so ill-treated her that even the tyrant kept his wrath grievous, thinking that the punishment for this was the greatest pledge of their fellowship with one another in the attack.

Alexander, hearing from Nearchus the prediction of the Chaldaeans, was dismayed, and, ever the more reckoning the shrewdness and renown of the men, was troubled in spirit. At last, sending most of his friends into the city, he himself, turning aside to another path, passed Babylon by, and, encamping two hundred stadia away, kept quiet. All marvelling, there came to him, among others, many of the Greeks and of the philosophers the school of Anaxarchus.

Dionysius, in the journey conjecturing what had happened, picked out the most trustworthy of the cavalry and the foot, with whom he hastened toward the city, falling short in no haste; for he reckoned it would not otherwise be possible to prevail over the cavalry unless he hastened; which he did. For if he should make his arrival more unexpectedly than they, he hoped easily to master the design; which indeed turned out.

These, learning the cause and using the arguments drawn from philosophy effectively, so changed him that he came to despise all divination, and most of all that honoured among the Chaldaeans. Therefore the king, as though wounded in spirit and healed by the words of the philosophers, entered Babylon with his force.

For the cavalry supposed that Dionysius would neither still depart nor remain at the camp; therefore, thinking they had mastered the design, they said that he had at Gela pretended to be fleeing from the Phoenicians, but now had in truth fled from the Syracusans.

The inhabitants, as before, receiving the soldiers humanely, all betook themselves to relaxation and luxury, a great abundance of provisions having been made ready. These things, then, were done in this year.

Dionysius, having traversed about four hundred stadia, was present about midnight at the gate of Achradina with a hundred cavalry and six hundred foot; finding it shut, he applied to it the reed brought down from the marshes, which the Syracusans are accustomed to use for the binding of the plaster. While the gates were being burned, he took up the latecomers.

At the time when Dionysius was most engaged in besieging Rhegium, the Celts dwelling beyond the Alps, passing through the narrows with great forces, seized the country between the Apennine and the Alpine mountains, casting out the Tyrrhenians who dwelt there. 113.2. These some say were colonized from the twelve cities in Tyrrhenia; but some say that Pelasgians, before the Trojan times fleeing from Thessaly the flood that occurred in the time of Deucalion, settled in this place. 113.3. The Celts, then, having divided the country by nations, the so-called Sennones happened to have received the place lying farthest from the mountains by the sea. This being scorching, and being ill at ease, they were eager to migrate, and arming the younger men sent them to seek a country in which they should dwell. Invading, then, Tyrrhenia, and being in number about thirty thousand, they plundered the country of the Clusini. 113.4. At which time the people of the Romans sent envoys to Tyrrhenia to spy out the army of the Celts. The envoys, coming to Clusium and seeing a battle taking place, becoming more brave than prudent, drew up with the Clusini against the besiegers. 113.5. One of the envoys having succeeded and slain one of the more notable commanders, the Celts, learning what had happened, sent envoys to Rome to demand the surrender of the envoy who had begun the unjust war. 113.6. The senate at first tried to persuade the envoys of the Celts to take money for the wrongs done; but when they would not give heed, they voted to give up the accused. But the father of him who was to be given up, being one of the military tribunes who had the consular authority, brought the case before the people, and being powerful with the multitude, persuaded them to make void the judgement of the senate. 113.7. The people, then, who in the times before had obeyed the senate in all things, now first began to dissolve the judgement decided by the senate. 114.1. The envoys of the Celts, coming to their own camp, reported the answer of the Romans. At which being greatly indignant, and taking in addition a force from their countrymen, they hastened against Rome itself, being more than seventy thousand. The military tribunes of the Romans, being in their own authority, and hearing of the onset of the Celts, armed all those of military age. 114.2. Going out in full force and crossing the Tiber, they led their force along the river eighty stades, and when the Gauls were reported to be approaching, they drew up the army. 114.3. The bravest, twenty-four thousand, they drew up from the river to the hills, while on the highest hills they stationed the weakest. The Celts, extending their phalanx far, whether by chance or by foresight, stationed the best on the hills. 114.4. At the same time the trumpets on both sides gave the signal, and the armies came together to battle with much shouting. The chosen of the Celts, drawn up against the weakest of the Romans, easily routed them from the hills. 114.5. Therefore, these fleeing in throngs to the Romans in the plain, the ranks were thrown into confusion, and the Celts pressing upon them, they fled in dismay. Most rushing to the river and in the confusion falling upon one another, the Celts did not fail to slay the hindmost continually; therefore the whole plain was strewn with corpses. 114.6. Of those who fled to the river, the bravest swam across with their arms, prizing their full armour equally with their lives; the current being violent, some, weighed down by the burden of their arms, were drowned, while others, after much hardship being carried for a considerable distance, were with difficulty saved. 114.7. The enemy pressing upon them and slaying many along the river, most of the survivors, throwing away their arms, swam across the Tiber. 115.1. The Celts, having slain many even by the river itself, did not even so desist from their eagerness, but hurled javelins at those swimming across. Many missiles being discharged into the throngs in the river, it came to pass that those who threw did not miss. Whence some, falling in with mortal wounds, immediately died, while others, wounded through, and through the flowing of blood and the violence of the current growing faint, were carried away. 115.2. Such a disaster having befallen the Romans, most of the survivors seized the city of Veii, lately razed by themselves, and fortified the place as best they could, and took in those saved from the flight; but a few of those who swam across, fleeing unarmed to Rome, announced that all had perished. Such great misfortunes being reported to those left in the city, all fell into perplexity; 115.3. for they reckoned that to withstand was impossible, all the young men having perished, and to flee with children and wives was too dangerous, the enemy being near. Many of the private persons, then, with their whole households fled to the neighbouring cities, while the magistrates of the city, encouraging the multitude, ordered them quickly to convey to the Capitol the grain and the rest of the necessaries. 115.4. This being done, both the citadel and the Capitol were full, apart from the things pertaining to food, of silver and gold and the most costly raiment, as though from the whole city the good things had been gathered into one place. They, then, conveyed what was possible of their goods and fortified the aforesaid place, having a respite of three days. 115.5. For the Celts on the first day were occupied in cutting off the heads of the dead according to their ancestral custom; and for two days, encamping by the city, and seeing the walls deserted, but perceiving an outcry being made, which those making it who were conveying the most useful things to the citadel, they supposed that the Romans were laying an ambush for them. 115.6. On the fourth day, learning the truth, they broke open the gates and laid waste the city, except for a few houses on the Palatine. After this, making assaults day by day on the strong places, they did no noteworthy harm to their opponents, while they lost many of their own; nevertheless they did not desist from their eagerness, hoping that, if they should not master it by force, they would in time, the necessaries wholly failing, wear them down.

When Agesias was archon at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Gaius Publius and Papirius; and the hundred and fourteenth Olympiad was held, in which Micinas of Rhodes won the foot-race. At this time there came envoys from nearly the whole inhabited world, some congratulating him on his successes, some crowning him, others establishing friendships and alliances, many bringing magnificent gifts, and some making their defence concerning the charges against them.

When the fire destroyed the gates, he with those who had followed rode in through Achradina, and the most powerful of the cavalry, hearing of what had happened, did not wait for the multitude, but immediately came out to the aid, being altogether few—they were about the marketplace—and, being encircled by the mercenaries, were all shot down.

For, apart from the nations and cities of Asia, and the rulers besides, many came also from Europe and Libya: from Libya the Carthaginians, the Libyphoenicians, and all who dwell along the coast as far as the Pillars of Heracles; and from Europe the cities of the Greeks sent envoys, and the Macedonians, and besides the Illyrians and most of those dwelling about the Adriatic, the Thracian peoples and of the neighbouring Gauls, whose race was then first known among the Greeks.

Dionysius, going over the city, killed those who came out scattered to the aid, and went to the houses of those hostilely disposed, of whom some he killed, others he cast out of the city. The rest of the multitude of the cavalry, driven out of the city, seized the place now called Aetna.

Alexander, having taken a register of the envoys, arranged to give the replies first to some and then to all the rest in order. And first he dealt with those who had come about the temples, second with those who came about the gifts, next with those who had disputes with their neighbours, fourth with those who came about private matters, and fifth with those who spoke against the return of the exiles.
At daybreak the multitude of the mercenaries and the army of the Sicilians came to Syracuse, but the Geloans and Camarinaeans, being at variance with Dionysius, departed to Leontini.

To the Eleians, then, he dealt first, then to the Ammonians, the Delphians, and the Corinthians, and besides to the Epidaurians and the rest, preferring the interviews according to the renown of their temples. Being eager to give to all the embassies pleasing replies, he sent them away satisfied so far as was possible.

. . . Therefore, compelled by the situation, Himilco sent a herald to Syracuse, urging the defeated to come to terms. Dionysius gladly listening, they made peace on these terms: that the Carthaginians, with the original colonists, should have the Elymi and Sicani; that the Selinuntians and Acragantines, and besides the Himeraeans, and besides these the Geloans and Camarinaeans, should dwell in unwalled cities and pay tribute to the Carthaginians; that the Leontines and Messenians and all the Sicels should be autonomous, and that the Syracusans should be ranged under Dionysius, and that those holding the captives and the ships should give them back to those who had lost them.

Having dismissed the embassies, he busied himself with the burial of Hephaestion. He took such pains over the care of the funeral that he not only surpassed all burials that had been before among men, but also left no possibility of surpassing it to those to come. For he had loved him most of those reputed in affection his friends, and after his death he honoured him beyond all surpassing. For, while he lived, he preferred him to all his friends, though Craterus held a rivalling friendship.

The treaties having been made, the Carthaginians sailed off to Libya, having lost more than half their soldiers from the disease; and none the less, the plague remaining in Libya too, a very great number both of the Carthaginians themselves and of the allies were destroyed.

The following are contained in the fourteenth of the books of Diodorus. The overthrow of the democracy at Athens and the establishment of the Thirty Men. The lawless conduct of the Thirty Men against the citizens. How Dionysius the tyrant, after building a citadel, divided the city and the land among the multitude. How Dionysius, when his tyranny was being dissolved, unexpectedly recovered it. How the Lacedaemonians ordered the affairs of Greece. The death of Alcibiades, and the tyranny of Clearchus the Laconian at Byzantium and its overthrow. How Lysander the Lacedaemonian, attempting to abolish the kings descended from Heracles, failed. How Dionysius reduced Catane and Naxos to slavery and removed the Leontines to Syracuse. The founding of Halaesa in Sicily. The war of the Lacedaemonians against the Eleians. How Dionysius built the wall by the Hexapyla. How Cyrus, marching against his brother, was slain. How the Lacedaemonians came to the aid of the Greeks in Asia. The founding of Adranum in Sicily, and the death of Socrates the philosopher. The building of the wall about the Chersonese. The preparation of Dionysius for the war against Carthage and his manufacture of arms, in the course of which the catapult missile was invented. How war broke out between the Carthaginians and Dionysius. How Dionysius took by siege Motye, a notable city of the Carthaginians. How the Aegestaeans burned the camp of Dionysius. How the Carthaginians, having crossed over to Sicily with three hundred thousand men, made war upon Dionysius. The withdrawal of Dionysius to Syracuse. The expedition of the Carthaginians to the strait, and the capture of Messene. A great sea-battle of the Carthaginians against Dionysius, and the victory of the Carthaginians. The plundering of the temples of Demeter and Core by the Carthaginians. The punishment from the gods upon the temple-robbers, and the destruction of the Carthaginian force by a pestilential plague. A sea-battle of the Syracusans against the Carthaginians and the victory of the Syracusans. The public speech of Theodorus concerning liberty. How Dionysius, by outgeneralling the thousand most turbulent mercenaries, brought it about that they were cut down. How Dionysius laid siege to the strongholds and the camp of the Carthaginians. How Dionysius, having stormed the Carthaginians, burned many of the enemy's ships. The defeat of the Carthaginians by land and by sea at once. The flight of the Carthaginians by night, Dionysius secretly aiding them, unknown to the Syracusans, for four hundred talents. The misfortunes that befell the Carthaginians on account of their impiety toward the divine. The resettlement of the cities in Sicily that had been laid waste. How Dionysius, of the Sicilian cities, took some by siege and brought others into alliance. How he concluded friendship with the rulers Agyris the Agyrinaean and Nicodemus the Centoripine. How Agesilaus the king of the Spartans crossed over into Asia with an army and laid waste the country subject to the Persians. How Agesilaus conquered the Persians in battle under the command of Pharnabazus. Concerning the Boeotian War and what was done in it. How Conon, appointed general by the Persians, rebuilt the walls of the Athenians. How the Lacedaemonians conquered the Boeotians near Corinth, and this war was called the Corinthian. How Dionysius, having broken into Tauromenium amid many dangers, was driven out. How the Carthaginians were defeated by Dionysius near the city of Bacaena. The expedition of the Carthaginians into Sicily and the conclusion of the war. How Thibron the Lacedaemonian, being general, was defeated by the Persians and slain. How Dionysius besieged Rhegium. How the Greeks of Italy, uniting into a single state, took the field against Dionysius. How Dionysius, having won the battle and taken ten thousand prisoners, released them without ransom and granted the cities their independence. The capture and razing of Caulonia and Hipponium and their removal to Syracuse. How the Greeks made the Peace of Antalcidas with Artaxerxes. The capture of Rhegium and the disasters that befell the city. The capture of Rome by the Gauls, except for the Capitol.

For when one of the Companions said that Craterus was loved no less than Hephaestion, he declared that Craterus was a lover of the king, but Hephaestion a lover of Alexander. And when the mother of Darius, at her first interview, through ignorance did obeisance to Hephaestion as being the king, and after recognizing her error was confounded, he said: “Do not be troubled, mother; for he too is Alexander.”

In general Hephaestion shared in such great power and friendly freedom of speech that, Olympias being ill-disposed toward him because of envy and in her letters rebuking him rather harshly and threatening, he wrote to her among other things reprovingly, and at the end of his letter set down this: “Cease being slandered to us, and do not be angry nor threaten; but if you will not, it will trouble us little; for you know that Alexander is above all.”

The king, then, preparing for the funeral, ordered the neighbouring cities to contribute, according to their ability, to the adornment of the funeral, and ordered all who dwelt in Asia carefully to quench what is called among the Persians the sacred fire, until he should accomplish the funeral; for this the Persians are accustomed to do at the deaths of their kings.

The multitude took the order for an evil omen and supposed that the divinity foretold the death of the king. There occurred also other strange signs foreshowing the death of Alexander, about which we shall speak a little later, when we have given the account of the funeral.

For each of the commanders and friends, aiming at the king's satisfaction, made images of ivory, gold, and the other things admired among men; and he himself, gathering the architects and a multitude of artisans, took down the wall for ten stadia, and, gathering up the baked brick and making level the place that was to receive the pyre, built a four-sided pyre, each side being a stadium long.

Dividing the place into thirty compartments and laying the roofs with the trunks of palm-trees, he made the whole structure square. After this he put around the whole circuit an adornment, of which the base was filled with golden prows of quinqueremes, two hundred and forty in number, having on their catheads two archers four cubits high kneeling on one knee, and statues five cubits high in full armour; and the spaces between were filled with felt purple cloths.

Above these the second level was supported by torches fifteen cubits high, having at the handle golden crowns, and at the place of flaming eagles with wings spread and looking downward, and beside the bases serpents looking up at the eagles. At the third circuit was wrought a multitude of animals of every kind being hunted.

Then the fourth level had a golden battle of centaurs, and the fifth golden lions and bulls alternately. The upper part was filled with Macedonian and barbarian arms, the one signifying deeds of valour, the others defeats. And over all stood Sirens, hollowed out and able secretly to receive those who were within them and sang a funeral dirge for the dead.

The height of the whole structure was more than a hundred and thirty cubits. In general, the commanders, all the soldiers, the envoys, and besides the inhabitants being eager about the adornment of the funeral, they say that the sum of the money spent came to more than twelve thousand talents.

In keeping with this magnificence, and the other honours done at the funeral, he finally ordered all to sacrifice to Hephaestion as a god assessor; for by chance there came one of his friends, Philip, bringing an oracle from Ammon to sacrifice to Hephaestion as a god. Therefore, becoming overjoyed that the god too had ratified his own opinion, he was the first to perform the sacrifice, and entertained the multitude splendidly, having sacrificed ten thousand victims of every kind.

The Romans being in such confusions, the neighbouring Tyrrhenians went over the country of the Romans with a strong force, plundering it, and gained possession of many persons and no little spoil. But those of the Romans who had fled to Veii, falling unexpectedly upon the Tyrrhenians, routed them, and took away the booty and mastered the camp. 116.2. Becoming masters of many arms, they distributed them to those who were unarmed, and gathering the men from the country they armed them; for they wished to deliver those who had fled together to the Capitol from the siege. 116.3. They being at a loss in what way they might make it known to those shut up, because the Celts were encamped about with great forces, a certain Cominius Pontius undertook to encourage those in the Capitol. 116.4. Setting out alone and swimming across the river by night, he came unseen to a certain rock of the Capitol hard to climb, and dragging himself up with difficulty by this, made known to those in the Capitol concerning those gathered at Veii, and that, watching for an opportunity, they would attack the Celts. Then, going down by the way he had come up and swimming across the Tiber, he returned to Veii. 116.5. But the Celts, observing the tracks of him who had lately come up, arranged to climb up the same rock by night. Therefore about midnight, the guards being careless of their watch because of the strength of the place, some of the Celts climbed up the rock. 116.6. They escaped the notice of the guards, but the sacred geese of Hera, that were kept there, seeing those climbing up, made an outcry. The guards running together to the place, these, struck with dismay, did not dare to come on; but a certain Marcus Manlius, a notable man, coming to the rescue at the place, with his sword cut off the hand of the one climbing up, and striking him in the breast with his shield rolled him off the rock. 116.7. Likewise too, the second, climbing up, perishing, the rest all quickly fled; and the rock being precipitous, all, being hurled down headlong, died. Therefore, the Romans sending an embassy about a settlement, they were persuaded, taking a thousand pounds of gold, to leave the city and to depart from the country of the Romans. 116.8. The Romans, their houses being razed and most of their citizens having perished, gave leave to whoever wished to build a house in whatever place he chose, and furnished public tiles, which to the present day are called "state-tiles." 116.9. All, then, building according to their own choice, it came to pass that the streets in the city became narrow and full of turns; therefore later, when they had increased, they were unable to make the streets straight. Some say also that the women, having contributed their golden ornament for the common safety, obtained for this honour from the people, so as to have the right to ride upon chariots through the city. 117.1. The Romans being humbled because of the aforesaid disaster, the Volsci carried war against them. The military tribunes of the Romans, then, enrolling soldiers and leading their force into the open, encamped in the place called Marcius, distant from Rome two hundred stades. 117.2. The Volsci being encamped opposite with a larger army and assaulting the camp, those in Rome, fearing for those in the camp, appointed Marcus Furius as dictator . . . 117.3. These, arming all those of military age, went out by night, and surprising at daybreak the Volsci as they assaulted the camp, appearing in their rear, they easily routed them. Those from the camp also coming out, the Volsci, cut off in the middle, were almost all cut down. Therefore those who in the time before seemed to be strong, because of this disaster became the weakest of the surrounding peoples. 117.4. After the battle the dictator, hearing that Bola was being plundered by the Aeculani, who are now called the Aecicli, leading his force slew most of the besiegers. Thence he broke camp to Sutrian territory, which was a colony, which the Tyrrhenians had seized by force. Falling suddenly upon the Tyrrhenians, he slew many of them and recovered the city for the Sutrians. 117.5. The Gauls who had departed from Rome plundering the city Veascium, an ally of the Romans, the dictator, attacking them and slaying most, mastered all the baggage, in which was also the gold that they had taken at Rome and almost all that had been plundered at the capture of the city. 117.6. Having accomplished so much, because of the envy of the tribunes of the people he was prevented from leading a triumph. Some, however, say that he led a triumph over the Tusci upon a white four-horse chariot, and that for this two years later he was condemned by the people to a heavy fine; concerning whom we shall make mention at the proper times. 117.7. Those of the Celts who had gone into Iapygia returned through the country of the Romans; and a little after, plotted against by night by the Cerii, they were all cut down in the Trausian plain. 117.8. Callisthenes the historian began to write his history from the peace made in this year between the Greeks and Artaxerxes the King of the Persians; and traversing a period of thirty years he wrote ten books, and ended the last of his work at the seizure of the temple at Delphi by Philomelus the Phocian. 117.9. We, since we are come to the peace made between the Greeks and Artaxerxes and to the danger of Rome from the Gauls, in accordance with the purpose set at the beginning, shall make this the end of this book.

The following are contained in the fifteenth of the books of Diodorus. How the Persians waged the war against Evagoras in Cyprus. How the Lacedaemonians, contrary to the common agreements, removed the Mantineans from their fatherland. Concerning the poems of Dionysius the tyrant. Concerning the arrest of Tiribazus and his acquittal. Concerning the death of Glos and the condemnation of Orontes. How Amyntas and the Lacedaemonians made war upon the Olynthians. How the Lacedaemonians seized the Cadmeia. How they enslaved the Greek cities contrary to the treaties. The founding of the island Pharos in the Adriatic. The expedition of Dionysius into Tyrrhenia and the plundering of the temple. The expedition of Dionysius against the Carthaginians, and a victory and a defeat. How the Thebans recovered the Cadmeia. How the Carthaginians, falling into a pestilential disease, were endangered. Concerning the Boeotian War and what was done in it. The expedition of the Triballi against Abdera. The expedition of the Persians against Egypt. How the Thebans, having conquered the Lacedaemonians in a most notable battle at Leuctra, laid claim to the leadership of the Greeks. What was done by the Thebans in their invasions of the Peloponnese. Concerning the training of Iphicrates and the things invented by him for campaigns. The expedition of the Lacedaemonians against Corcyra. Concerning the earthquake and flood that occurred about the Peloponnese, and the torch that appeared in the heavens. How among the Argives there occurred a great slaughter called the clubbing. Concerning Jason the tyrant of Pherae and his successors. The resettlement of Messene by the Thebans. The expedition of the Boeotians into Thessaly.

After the funeral, the king having turned to relaxation and a festal life, and seeming then to be strongest and most prosperous, destiny took away the time of life granted him by nature. At once the divinity too signified his death, many strange omens and signs occurring.

For, while the king was being anointed and the royal robe and diadem had been laid upon a certain throne, one of the inhabitants who was in bonds was loosed from his fetters of his own accord, and, escaping the guards' notice, passed through the doors of the court unhindered.

Coming to the throne and putting on the royal robe and the diadem, he sat down upon the throne and kept quiet. When the deed was discovered, the king, dismayed at the strangeness, came to the throne, and, without consternation, quietly questioned the man, who he was and with what intent he had done this.

When he said that he knew absolutely nothing, the king, referring the sign to the seers, killed him according to their judgement, so that the ill things signified might turn upon that man; and he himself, taking up the robe and sacrificing to the gods who avert evil, was in distress, and remembered the prediction of the Chaldaeans, and blamed the philosophers who had persuaded him to enter Babylon, and marvelled at the art of the Chaldaeans and the shrewdness of the men, and in general reviled those who by their ingenious arguments tried to outwit the power of destiny.

A little later the divinity set before him another sign concerning his kingdom. For, as he wished to view the lake about Babylon and was sailing with his friends in certain skiffs, for some days the ship, having been separated from the other boats, wandered alone, so that he even despaired of safety;

then, as he was sailing through a narrow channel closely covered with trees, and some of them overhung, his diadem was lifted off by these and fell again into the lake, and one of the rowers, swimming up and wishing to save the diadem safely, set it on his head and swam to the boat.
Having wandered three days and as many nights, he was saved; and, having put on the diadem again contrary to expectation, he once more referred to the seers concerning what was foreshown.

These urging him to perform magnificent sacrifices to the gods with all haste, he was invited by one of his friends, Medius the Thessalian, to come to a revel; and there, having taken much unmixed wine, at the last, having filled a great cup in honour of Heracles, he drank it off.

Suddenly, as though struck by some violent blow, he groaned aloud with a great cry, and was led away by his friends, supported by the hand. At once those in charge of the attendance received him, laid him down, and watched by him carefully;

but, the affliction increasing and the physicians being called together, no one was able to help him; and, gripped by many sufferings and dreadful pains, when he had given up life, taking off his ring, he gave it to Perdiccas.

When his friends asked, “To whom do you leave the kingdom?” he said, “To the strongest”; and he added, uttering this as his last word, that all the foremost of his friends would hold a great funeral contest in his honour.

He, then, died in the manner described, having reigned twelve years and seven months, and having accomplished the greatest deeds, not only of those who reigned before him, but also of those who would come after, down to our own time. But since some of the historians have differed about the death of this king, declaring that the death came about through a deadly poison, we think it necessary not to pass over their accounts.

For they say that Antipater, who had been left by him as general in Europe, fell out with Olympias the king's mother; and at first he despised her, because Alexander did not receive the slanders against him, but afterward, the enmity ever increasing — the king, through his piety toward the divine, wishing to gratify his mother in all things — he gave many indications of his estrangement toward him; and besides this, the slaughter of Parmenion and Philotas striking horror into the friends, he gave a deadly poison to drink to the king through his own son, who was appointed about the cup.

After the death he had the greatest power in Europe, and after this his son Cassander succeeded to the kingdom; therefore many historians did not dare to write about the poisoning. But it became clear by the very deeds that Cassander was most hostilely disposed toward the affairs of Alexander; for, having murdered Olympias, he cast her out unburied, and rebuilt with much zeal the Thebes that had been razed by Alexander.

After the death of the king, Sisyngambris the mother of Darius, having greatly bewailed both the death of Alexander and her own desolation, at the last verge of her life held out against food and on the fifth day ended her life, sorrowfully indeed, but not ingloriously laying down her life.
And we, having come to the death of Alexander, shall, according to the purpose set forth at the beginning of the book, attempt to go through the deeds of his successors in the books that follow.
